So far, the known weakest assumption for 2QKE is the existence of one-way functions (OWFs). Can we construct 2QKE from a weaker assumption than OWFs? In this paper, we give the first complete characterization of 2QKE. We show that the following four primitives are (existentially) equivalent: everlasting-secure 2QKE, standard 2QKE, efficiently-verifiable state puzzles (EV-StatePuzzs), and one-time secure digital signatures with quantum signatures and signing keys. Because EV-StatePuzzs are potentially weaker than OWFs [Kretschmer, Qian and Tal 2025], the equivalence implies that 2QKE are potentially weaker than OWFs. Moreover, our result shows the equivalence between standard 2QKE and everlasting-secure 2QKE, which means that everlasting security comes for free. Finally, one-shot signatures, quantum lightning, and public-key quantum money mini-schemes imply EV-StatePuzzs, and therefore, our result also gives a new lowerbound, namely everlasting-secure 2QKE, of these public-key unclonable primitives. We also show that one-shot signatures imply QPKE with quantum public keys. [Kitagawa, Morimae,Nishimaki and Yamakawa, 2024] constructed QPKE with quantum public keys from OWFs, and it was open whether QPKE with quantum public keys can be constructed from an assumption weaker than or incomparable to OWFs. Our result gives a potential answer to this question since one-shot signatures seem to be incomparable with OWFs. Moreover, QPKE constructed from one-shot signatures has an additional functionality, which we call certified freeze, that allows the receiver to publish a publicly verifiable classical certificate that computationally binds the receiver to an upper bound on the total number of distinct valid ciphertexts under its verification key.

papers.title: Enforcing Accountable Disclosure in Confidential AI
papers.summary: Advances in CPU and GPU confidential computing enable confidential AI, allowing LLMs to process user prompts without exposing them to service providers or infrastructure operators. However, AI agents often need to send prompt-derived information to external services, and providers may also require limited disclosure for safety monitoring and failure diagnosis. We propose CORDE, a system for confidential virtual machines (CVMs) designed to satisfy the principle of Confine or Declare: user-derived data is confined by default, but when necessary, it may leave the CVM only after being "declared." To "declare" data is to record its exact contents, recipient, and stated reason in a user-accessible, tamper-evident declaration log. To put this principle into practice, we present an integrated system design that combines per-user information-flow control in Rust with a TEE-based ledger and remote attestation. Our evaluation on an NVIDIA H100 GPU shows that declaration before disclosure adds little overhead in task latency, about 0.5% on the AppWorld agent benchmark. CORDE provides a basis for accountable disclosure of user data, supporting responsible and transparent data management in AI services.

papers.title: Prior-data fitted networks for variable selection
papers.summary: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) have become state-of-the-art for tabular prediction but remain underexplored in other areas of statistics. In this work, we present two PFNs for Bayesian variable selection: CD-PFN identifies conditional dependencies, and PC-PFN identifies parents and children in a causal graph. Both networks estimate posterior inclusion probabilities (PIPs) without posterior samples or data-specific modeling. In semi-synthetic and real data experiments, CD-PFN and PC-PFN often outperform existing methods, demonstrating the value of PFNs for variable selection and their potential in statistics more broadly. Open-source software is available.

papers.title: Robots in the City: Persona-Based Perceptions of Urban Robots
papers.summary: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street remains unclear. We examine how robot presence and type affect perceived safety across urban contexts. We generate 18 images of Seoul streets that vary in time of day, road class, and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid). Two multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, choose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents complete the same task. Both models prefer streets without robots and favor the delivery robot over the humanoid. Robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, whereas road class has smaller effects. In the model rationales, the delivery robot appears as a physical obstacle, whereas the humanoid appears as either a threat or a source of protection. Like humans, both models chose robots more often at night, but chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often, and Gemma showed a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans. These results show that the effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and that persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.

papers.title: Gravitational-Wave Microlensing as a Probe of Compact Object Population
papers.summary: The abundance of compact objects ranging from stellar to intermediate masses ($\sim 1 - 10^{5}M_{\odot}$) remains poorly constrained, particularly for populations such as primordial black holes and dark matter subhalos that emit little or no electromagnetic radiation. Gravitational-wave (GW) microlensing provides a complementary way to probe these populations through wave-optics effects imprinted on the GW signals, with implications for astrophysical and cosmological inference. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework to infer the population properties of microlenses from an ensemble of microlensed GW events, constraining the slope of the power-law lens mass function ($α_{\rm ML}$), the lens number density ($n_0$), and the fraction of dark matter in compact lenses ($f_{\rm DM}$). Using simulated microlensed GW signals drawn from a realistic binary black hole population, we find that $\sim 100$ detected microlensed events are able to constrain both $α_{\rm ML}$ and $n_0$, although a degeneracy between the two remains. For a low-mass-dominated lens population ($α_{\rm ML}=2$) with $n_0=10^6~\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, a three-year observation at the O4 sensitivity yields $\sim 130$ detectable microlensed events and recovers the injected dark-matter fraction, $f_{\rm DM}\simeq 1.2 \times 10^{-4}$, with a 90% credible interval of $7.3 \times 10^{-5} \lesssim f_{\rm DM} \lesssim 1.8 \times 10^{-4}$.

papers.title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials
papers.summary: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.
papers.comment: Oral presentation at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on World Models for High-Stakes Health. 31 pages, 5 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/alicemkyn/ivbench

papers.title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating
papers.summary: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.

papers.title: Compiling, Validating, and Using Human Reference Atlas Cell Type Annotation Crosswalks
papers.summary: The Human Reference Atlas (HRA) v2.5 includes 4,807 anatomical structures, 1,347 cell types, and 2,215 biomarkers (genes, proteins, lipids); 81 organs with 1,392 anatomical structures modeled in three dimensions (3D). Mapping new data into the HRA requires 3D spatial registration and/or cell type annotation (CTann). Many CTann tools exist but few use cell type names linked to Cell Ontology (CL), making comparisons across tools, tissues, and organs difficult. The HRA supports five transcriptomics CTann tools (Azimuth, CellTypist, popV, FR-Match, Pan-Human Azimuth), four sc-proteomics CTann tools (DeepCell Types, DeepCell Types-HuBMAP, Robust Image-Based Cell Annotator [RIBCA], and SpaTial cELl LeARning [STELLAR]), plus a Cell Distance Explorer (CDE) Spatial Omics collection covering previously published annotations across 12 tissue types with 47,349,496 cells. Assigned cell types differ in number, resolution, and coverage. This paper details how 10 crosswalks were constructed, validated, and used to compile a "Supertree" that can be used to compare CTann across organs and technologies in support of reference atlas constitution and usage. All data and code can be accessed at https://cns-iu.github.io/hra-ctann-supporting-information.

papers.title: Right, Wrong, or Unfinished: A Competing Risks Framework for Language-Model Reasoning under Token Budgets
papers.summary: Assessing language-model performance under a token budget requires understanding both when a response will finish and whether it will be correct. We develop Competing Risks Analysis of Token Expenditure in Reasoning (CRATER), a statistically principled framework that treats correct and incorrect completion as distinct competing event types and responses unfinished at the generation limit as administratively right-censored. The fitted distribution provides probabilities of correct completion, incorrect completion, and remaining unfinished across token budgets, together with expected token consumption. We evaluate the proposed method using responses to MATH questions and demonstrate its value in two downstream applications. For routing before generation, CRATER guides the joint choice of a model configuration and token budget. Under hypothetical token prices, it reduces mean cost by $53.39 \%$ relative to a strong reference, with observed correctcompletion rates of $96.42 \%$ and $97.30 \%$, respectively. For repeated sampling, we combine CRATER's single-attempt success probabilities with an existing beta-binomial calibration approach to predict pass@k. Across both applications, CRATER delivers predictions at any specified token budget up to the generation limit from a common model of completion time and correctness, eliminating the need for separate parameter estimation for each budget.

papers.title: Spurious center-of-mass mode as an $S$-matrix pole within the Jost-random-phase approximation
papers.summary: Within the Jost-random-phase approximation (Jost-RPA), the spurious center-of-mass mode is a zero of the Jost determinant and hence a pole of the $S$ matrix. A zero at zero excitation energy $E$, whether from self-consistency or from a calibration of the residual interaction, is a pole of exactly second order when it has a single independent solution, every unoccupied bound orbital lies above the holes, and each hole is paired with every allowed partial wave; the order follows from the position of the zero, not from self-consistency. The state of this double pole, given by the Autonne-Takagi factorization of its $E^{-2}$ coefficient, is the zero-energy solution normalized by its inertia. In a self-consistent model of one energy density of the neutron and proton densities, every physical $S$-matrix element continued to $E=0$ carries the $E^{-2}$ term, contrary to an earlier conclusion. Subtracting the mode's principal part from the response changes the strength at real $E\neq0$ only through the smoothing and, in such a model, coincides with the projection of the ideal spurious state. In uncalibrated Woods-Saxon models of $^{16}$O and $^{208}$Pb the mode is a pair of poles on the imaginary axis.

papers.title: Doubly robust win statistics for hierarchical survival endpoints in individual- and cluster-randomized trials
papers.summary: Prioritized composite endpoints compare trial participants according to a prespecified clinical hierarchy, and the win estimands are increasingly used to summarize treatment effects. When the component event times are right-censored, a pairwise comparison may remain unresolved, and treating unresolved pairs as ties yields a win statistic whose value depends on the censoring distribution. We define win, loss, and tie probabilities at a fixed restriction time for prioritized time-to-event outcomes in individual-randomized trials and extend them to cluster-randomized trials, where cluster-average and individual-average estimands assign equal weight to clusters and to participants, respectively. We propose doubly robust estimators that combine inverse probability of censoring weighting with joint outcome models to incorporate information recorded before censoring. Under covariate-dependent censoring, the resulting U-statistics are consistent when either the censoring models or joint outcome models are correctly specified for both treatment arms, but not necessarily both. We establish asymptotic normality and derive analytic variance estimators for computationally efficient inference. Simulation studies under both designs evaluate bias, precision, and confidence interval coverage under working model misspecification. Applications to two real-world studies demonstrate the use of the proposed methods under individual- and cluster-randomized trials.

papers.title: Sure Enough to Share? Overconfidence in GenAI Video Discernment is Associated with Sharing Intentions
papers.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is blurring the line between synthesized and recorded videos, but less is known about people's awareness of their discernment abilities and the consequences of miscalibration. This study examines three forms of overconfidence in GenAI video discernment (i.e., overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision) and their associations with source judgments and sharing intentions in an online study (N = 973). Participants evaluated videos depicting everyday scenes and achieved 62.5% accuracy. Three forms of overconfidence showed distinct patterns: participants overplaced themselves by 12.8 percentile points, but overprecision showed consistent positive associations with sharing intentions and the tendency to classify videos as human-made. Age, GenAI usage, and AI literacy showed consistent positive associations with all three forms of overconfidence. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing the three forms of overconfidence to better understand GenAI engagement and incorporating metacognition into interventions to support informed media consumption.

papers.title: A Hybrid Approach for Automated Security Pattern Recovery
papers.summary: Security-by-design emphasises integrating security into software design and development. Security pattern catalogues operationalise this principle by prescribing reusable architectural solutions to recurring security problems. However, recovering their implementations from source code remains challenging because security patterns are abstract, span multiple components, and admit many valid implementations. We present SecPatRec, a hybrid approach for automated security pattern recovery from source code repositories. We treat a security pattern as a reference architecture and frame its recovery as a deductive task: determining which prescribed roles are present, grounding them in code entities, and recovering their interaction sequences. SecPatRec pairs a ReAct-style LLM agent equipped with semantic and lexical code search for role detection and grounding with static code property graph analysis for interaction recovery. We curate a human-validated ground-truth dataset of 100 pattern instances covering five security patterns across 93 open-source Java and Python repositories, and introduce a three-level evaluation framework measuring recovery correctness against this ground truth. We evaluate SecPatRec using four LLMs, including proprietary and open-source models. Averaged over all models and pattern instances, SecPatRec achieves role-detection accuracy of 0.84, role-grounding similarity of 0.84, and an interaction-recovery score of 0.66. Compared to a one-shot end-to-end LLM baseline, SecPatRec achieves higher aggregate recovery scores and lower estimated LLM API costs per run, while processing repositories that exceed the baseline's configured input limit. The recovered role mappings and statically derived interaction sequences provide structural and behavioural evidence that can support inspection of security-pattern implementations.

papers.title: GRIDSHIELD: Verifiable Grid Feasibility and Manipulation Resistance in Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading
papers.summary: Blockchain-based peer-to-peer (P2P) energy markets let neighbors trade directly, but concentrate unchecked power in the clearing operator. Most prior work addresses only part of this: network-aware clearing respects grid constraints but operates on plaintext allocations, while privacy-preserving designs hide bids yet either drop the network constraint, enforce it only inside an unauditable computation, or recover it at the cost of a per-circuit trusted setup. Neither considers what happens if an adversary captures the operator's clearing privilege to reorder trades for profit or curtail a rival. We present GRIDSHIELD, a P2P energy-trading system that clears sealed bids with an order-independent batch program, removing the welfare a compromised operator can extract by reordering trades, and proves the result grid-feasible via an aggregated congestion-feasibility proof (ACFP). Exploiting the additive homomorphism of Pedersen commitments, ACFP reconstructs each grid constraint directly from per-bus commitments, reducing feeder-wide feasibility verification over any public grid constraints to a single aggregated range proof over the hidden allocation, with a reveal-and-recompute challenge that catches feasible yet unfair clearings. We introduce congestion-responsibility fairness (CRF), a metric scoring curtailment against each party's physical responsibility for congestion rather than consumption. We evaluate GRIDSHIELD against three prior P2P energy-trading designs across four feeders, including a 240-node Midwest feeder with real hourly loads, on a live Hyperledger Fabric network benchmarked with Hyperledger Caliper. GRIDSHIELD proves an entire round feasible with a few-kilobyte proof and no trusted setup, rejects infeasible allocations two of the three compared designs accept, and sustains $\approx$1064 tx/s.

papers.title: Uncertainty aware prediction from incomplete clinical records: a conformal prediction study of Parkinsonian classification using C-OPN data
papers.summary: Background: Incomplete clinical records and imbalanced diagnostic groups complicate Parkinsonian classification. We examined whether incomplete records could support useful lists of diagnostic possibilities through conformal prediction, assessing how often the lists retained the recorded diagnosis, their length and the uncertainty remaining. Methods: We analyzed records from 3,434 Canadian Open Parkinson Network participants: 2,853 with Parkinson's disease, 171 in the atypical Parkinsonian group (AP) and 410 healthy controls. In three repeats of five-fold cross-validation, we compared single-category predictions, conformal prediction sets and lists combined across 21 analyses using alternative models and assumptions about missing entries. An information deficit score summarized unavailable information. Results: The median proportion of eligible predictor entries unrecorded per participant was 75.6%. Single-category prediction correctly classified 89.29% of test records (balanced accuracy 55.40%), but only 10.33% of AP records. Conformal prediction sets included the recorded category in 93.35% of evaluation records and averaged 1.846 categories; combined lists increased inclusion to approximately 99% and averaged 2.289 categories. AP inclusion increased from 98.05% to 100%. Combined lists averaged 1.010 more categories in the group with the greatest information deficit than in the group with the least (95% interval 0.996-1.023). Conclusions: Even with extensive missing information and imbalanced diagnostic groups, clinical records can support informative prediction when uncertainty is quantified and expressed through sets of possible diagnoses rather than a single label. Joint assessment of list length and information deficit showed both the narrowing achieved and the records for which all three categories remained open.
authors: for the Canadian Open Parkinson Network
papers.comment: Main manuscript: 31 pages, 6 figures. Supplements S1-S5: 37 pages, 2 figures. A combined supplement is also provided as an ancillary PDF

papers.title: When File Ingestion Misleads Language Models: Measuring and Mitigating Divergences in Office Documents
papers.summary: Office documents are now routinely uploaded to large language models (LLMs) for processing. However, an LLM does not always see what a human sees, because it typically reads the text that an extractor produces from the document's underlying Office Open XML (OOXML) files. Depending on the implementation, extractors differ in which OOXML parts they read and how they interpret them, so their output can differ from what Office applications display. For example, by slightly shifting the positions of text boxes on a slide, an adversary can swap the order in which the model reads them while the slide looks unchanged. We show that this extraction divergence is an attack surface for LLM applications. In this work, we first measure what an adversary can exploit by analyzing the widely used extractors that LLM applications rely on. By combining static source code analysis with dynamic analysis, we identify 19 OOXML channels where extractors read content a human cannot see and 12 where they drop content a human can. We also find that widely used extractors ignore display formatting and reading order, so even visible content reaches the model in a different form. Building on these findings, we construct five attacks that lead the model to interpret a document differently from a human reviewer, without injecting any instruction. We test the attacks on four major chat assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Microsoft 365 Copilot) and four coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity, and GitHub Copilot CLI), and every one of them is misled by at least one attack. Finally, we propose Prism, a lightweight defense that reconstructs the human view from the OOXML specification before passing the text to the model. Prism also generalizes to unseen attack payloads.

papers.title: Unsupervised Neural Operators for Rotating Relativistic Stars: High-Fidelity Equation of State Inference and Pulsar Spin Evolution at Scale
papers.summary: Observed populations of rotating neutron stars~(NSs) with millisecond-order periods are powerful probes of fundamental physics. Mass-radius measurements inform poorly constrained properties of degenerate nuclear matter, whereas high-fidelity population synthesis connects unknowns in NS formation and binary evolution to large radio-timing surveys. However, repeated structure calculations are prohibitive due to the computational cost of solving the highly coupled partial differential equations of axisymmetric general relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium that govern rotating NS interiors. Non-rotating calculations or approximate rotational corrections can bias equation of state inference and limit the fidelity of population synthesis in tracing the evolutionary history of progenitors and propagating equation of state uncertainties. In this \textit{Letter}, we develop physics-informed neural operators that can solve the axisymmetric problem with high accuracy and negligible computational cost. \textit{Our solvers are trained in a fully unsupervised setting, with the training objective informed solely by the partial differential equations, and achieve a $10^3\times$ speed-up with negligible accuracy loss}. These solvers enable scalable EoS inference that self-consistently accounts for rotation and repeated stellar-structure calculations during binary evolution, making spin predictions that account for rotational structure and EoS uncertainties computationally accessible to population synthesis.

papers.title: Timing is Everything: Inferring Temporal Membership in Continually Updated Models
papers.summary: Continual model updating has become a common practice in the deployment of machine learning systems. However, the dynamic training behaviors give rise to new risks not sufficiently addressed by existing studies. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of temporal privacy risk in continually updated deep learning models. We formalize the notion of temporal membership in continually updated models. We then define the temporal membership inference attack, which seeks to infer whether and when individual samples were involved in model training, at both timestamp-level and interval-level granularities. To this end, we propose TMIA, a novel black-box attack that leverages bidirectional LSTMs to infer temporal membership from model outputs observed across successive updates. Through extensive experiments on three language models and three image classification models, we show that TMIA is highly effective and significantly outperforms existing baselines. Finally, we evaluate three potential defenses, revealing the trade-off between privacy protection and model utility.

papers.title: Private Vulnerability Testing for User Oversharing
papers.summary: Users can inadvertently increase their vulnerability to privacy attacks by oversharing personal information. In particular, the combination of individually innocuous attributes can place a user in a sufficiently small population to enable linkage or re-identification attacks. We present a privacy-preserving mechanism that allows users to determine whether the information they disclose places them below a predefined population threshold, without revealing their query or the data of other users. Our setting presents several practical challenges: users contributing data may be offline when queries are made, queries may select arbitrary subsets of attributes, and neither server should learn the queried population or its size. We address these challenges using secret-shared data and queries, private equality testing, and secure threshold computation. Our protocol provides computational privacy against a malicious client and semi-honest, non-colluding servers, while supporting arbitrary queries and dynamic database updates. We define reactive $f$-privacy for a dynamically evolving database and prove that our construction satisfies it, with the sequence of permitted threshold outputs defining the information available to the adversary across an execution. We optimise the protocol using oblivious-transfer extensions and pre-computation, achieving sub-second online query times for 96-bit queries on datasets of up to one million records.

papers.title: Neural Score-Driven Volatility and Risk Forecasting
papers.summary: We develop a score-driven volatility model in which no particular parametric innovation distribution needs to be specified. The proposed method relies on a lightweight neural network to represent the negative score of the innovation density. By integrating and normalizing the learned score and imposing location-scale identification, we recover a flexible innovation density that can accommodate asymmetry, including negative skewness commonly observed in financial returns. Two estimation procedures are considered. A two-step procedure estimates the neural score by score matching and subsequently fits the volatility recursion with the identified density held fixed. A one-step procedure jointly refines the neural and volatility parameters under the conditional likelihood. We illustrate the practical relevance of the proposed method using eight international equity indices, with a separate evaluation of the high-volatility first half of 2020. The results show that the neural score-driven models are competitive with Gaussian and Student-$t$ GAS benchmarks that require a prespecified parametric innovation distribution, with particularly strong performance during the COVID-19 period.

papers.title: Exact teleportation bounds for fermionic Hawking thermality beyond the single-mode approximation
papers.summary: Fermionic teleportation near a Schwarzschild horizon involves two physically distinct ingredients that are often varied together: Hawking thermal mixing and the relative composition of the right and left Unruh modes. We separate them by factorizing the reduced map of the detected exterior fermionic mode into a mode-preparation channel and a Hawking thermal channel. At fixed right-left Unruh-mode composition, we then solve a global constrained quantum-channel optimization over all two-qubit resource states whose fully entangled fraction remains at or below the standard teleportation threshold immediately before thermal mixing. A parity twirl and positivity reduce the arbitrary-state problem exactly to a two-variable quadratic optimization. The solution yields a necessary-and-sufficient activation boundary, a second exact boundary for attaining the universal optimum, and explicit optimizing states. The resulting phase diagram contains a strict no-go region, a composition-limited activation region, and a universal-bound region. The analysis converts state-specific observations of Hawking-assisted teleportation into exact channel-level bounds over the full two-qubit state space.

papers.title: Priced In or Bet On? Cram-School Lessons, Jeonse Leases, and Expected Appreciation in Seoul
papers.summary: South Korean families spend heavily on hagwons, private cram schools that prepare students for the university entrance exam. This paper asks what access to them is worth in housing and whether the premium includes expected appreciation. Using 2,197,510 Seoul apartment sales and jeonse (lump-sum deposit lease) contracts from 2015 to 2026, located with a new business-address geocoder, the analysis compares flats within the same middle-school assignment zone and month. Flats near hagwons preparing high-school students for the exam sell and lease for more: moving from the median complex to the 97th percentile of such hagwons within 500 meters is associated with sale prices 11.8% and jeonse deposits 7.3% higher, or 5.6% and 5.9% with complex size held fixed. Hagwons teaching younger children add no sale premium once these are held fixed. A larger premium in deposits than in prices across complexes reflects convenience: buyers pay less than renters to live near shops and services, above all repair and personal services. For the same flat type, complex and month, hagwon access produces no detectable change in the jeonse-to-price ratio, although the test detects the reconstruction value of old buildings; nearby shops raise it. Hagwon access is thus capitalized in proportion into prices and deposits, as expected of a current-flow amenity without extra expected appreciation. New tenants pay no lasting premium over renewing tenants, and deposits did not respond to major education-policy announcements. The housing premium is a cost of the education race that measures of tutoring spending omit.

papers.title: Local Whittle estimation for distributional time series: A regularization framework in Bayes Hilbert space
papers.summary: We study local Whittle estimation of long memory in density-valued time series in Bayes Hilbert space. The centered log-ratio (clr) transformation maps densities to a linear Hilbert space, allowing analysis using standard Hilbert space methods. When densities are reconstructed from finite samples, however, small absolute estimation errors can remain large relative to the true density in low-density tails. Taking logarithms can amplify this noise and introduce systematic distortions that affect memory estimation. We develop a framework for regularizing estimated densities before transformation to improve finite-sample performance while preserving the latent memory target. Using the clr representation, we apply local Whittle estimation to principal component scores along an estimated leading direction of the long-run covariance operator. The framework is based on local Whittle admissibility, defined by uniform asymptotic equivalence between the feasible and latent-score criteria. We separate density-estimation error from the population perturbation induced by regularization and give sufficient admissibility conditions based on density-estimation rates and the temporal dependence of the error components. Under suitable regularity assumptions, these conditions yield consistency for the latent memory parameter. We study additional tail smoothing, a vanishing density floor, and their combination. Monte Carlo experiments show that these procedures can reduce finite-sample bias relative to unregularized kernel density reconstruction. An application to daily distributions of intraday EUR/USD exchange rate returns illustrates the methodology.

papers.title: BobFlow: Towards Human-Agent Collaborative Data Science Using Dataflows
papers.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have established human-agent collaboration as a promising paradigm for data science. Effective collaboration requires a shared computational abstraction that enables agents to reason about processing logic while allowing human analysts to understand, guide, and refine the analysis. Although scripts written in Python or SQL provide precise control, their syntax and execution details can be difficult for analysts to understand and modify. In this paper, we argue that dataflows are an effective abstraction for human-agent collaboration in data science. We introduce BobFlow, a system that combines the dataflow abstraction with the ReAct paradigm. It enables agents to iteratively construct and execute dataflows for data science tasks while allowing analysts to inspect the analysis and provide feedback. Our user study shows that BobFlow helps analysts understand, inspect, and verify agent-generated analyses. A thorough experimental evaluation across proprietary and open-weight LLMs shows accuracy score gains of up to 18.6 points at just over 1/3 of a script-based ReAct agent's inference cost.

papers.title: Follow or Surpass? Collaboration, Sound, and the Recognition of Influence in Lineages of Jazz Trumpet Players
papers.summary: Cultural fields cohere not only horizontally, through collaboration, but also vertically, through lineages of artistic influence. Considerable attention has been devoted to collaboration networks in various fields of creative production; however, we know less about the structure of artistic influence that is nevertheless key to individual artistic development and the evolution of genres. We examine the structure of such an influence network in a genealogy of 52 prominent jazz trumpet players, combining musicians' discographies, demographic characteristics, geographical locations, and audio analysis of more than 16,000 recordings with exponential random graph models. Direct collaboration, overlap in collaborators, and sonic context similarity, that is, the similarity of the recordings on which players appear, are each associated with an ascribed influence tie, net of the others. Not surprisingly, ascribed ties connect musicians whose recordings share a similar sonic context, but musicians also tend to collaborate with their influences and share collaborators with them. However, players whose recordings share a sonic context and who move in the same circle of collaborators can be thought of as peers or rivals, rather than as influences of each other, because lineage implies a succession predicated on difference as much as on continuity. Taken together, our findings suggest that a field's account of its own evolution is neither a record of who played together nor a map of shared sonic contexts, but a selective ordering that requires both. While our data do not permit a causal account, our aim is to provide a rich and varied methodological strategy and descriptive as well as inferential tools to understand the yet understudied vertical integration of cultural fields through influence ties.

papers.title: Pairing Expert Critique with LLM-Driven Refinement: An Iterative Approach for Curating Quality AI Evaluation Datasets
papers.summary: Evaluating and improving domain-specific LLM responses requires high-quality reference data and rubrics, yet expert authoring is slow and expensive, and synthetic datasets may fail to capture practitioner preferences unless they are grounded in expert judgment. We present SME-C (Subject Matter Expert Critique), a human-AI workflow that captures expertise through lightweight critiques of candidate responses and complements it with LLM-driven analysis and refinement to iteratively curate response datasets and evaluation rubrics. We validate SME-C in the domain of financial business briefs, collecting 3,853 critiques from 411 finance professionals on 520 queries across two survey rounds. We evaluate two LLM-driven refinement strategies: one guided by the experts' written critiques and one that infers critique solely from their preference votes. In a blind validation survey with 100 additional professionals, we found that both strategies significantly improved quality over the experts' top-ranked baseline responses. The gains were concentrated among weaker original responses, and the two strategies excelled in different ways: critique-based refinement produced more domain-grounded improvements, whereas vote-based refinement was more effective at identifying and removing irrelevant content. The resulting rubrics and refined dataset support reproducible offline evaluation and benchmarking of LLMs, suggesting that structured expert critique is a viable alternative to expert authoring for building high-quality, domain-specific evaluation resources more quickly, at scale, and at lower cost.

papers.title: The Cosmology of Hawking Axions
papers.summary: Since primordial black holes (PBH) are always non-relativistic, their cosmological energy fraction grows relative to that of radiation. Thus, for even a tiny initial PBH abundance, the universe generically enters an epoch of early matter domination, which ends when the PBH evaporate to restore the hot big bang. We consider the possibility that a PBH dominated era yields a population of boosted axion-like particles (ALPs) produced from Hawking evaporation. Eventually these ``Hawking axions" become non-relativistic and decay to photons, which can affect various cosmological and astrophysical observables. Here we place new constraints on these particles through their impact on big bang nucleosynthesis, cosmic microwave background, large-scale structure, and X-ray observables. Furthermore, if Hawking axions remain relativistic through recombination, then depending on the progenitor PBH mass, they contribute $ΔN_{\rm eff}\simeq0.05$-$0.11$, which may be observable with future CMB probes.

papers.title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
papers.summary: Two foundational aspects of human cognition, abstractness and gender, are typically examined as separable. Here, we find they are systematically linked throughout the entire space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet -- and across numerous measurement techniques -- more abstract concepts are more associated with men, an effect which replicates in languages around the world. This pattern not only holds across conceptual domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, this bias emerges in human and AI responses in free association tasks, indicating its internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. The male abstraction bias may underlie and unify a range of stereotypes, evidencing gender as a core organizing dimension in conceptual space.

papers.title: Balance-Guided Forest for Causal Effect Estimation
papers.summary: Covariate balancing is widely used for estimating causal effects in observational studies. A central challenge is determining which covariate features should be balanced. Forest-kernel balancing provides a data-driven way to learn informative balancing features. Existing forest-kernel balancing methods first learn a tree-based representation and then construct balancing weights. However, this procedure creates a mismatch, as limited tree capacity may be spent on features that are already well represented. We propose Balance-Guided Forest (BGF), which uses the current balancing weights to guide subsequent tree construction. BGF grows trees using a novel splitting score that combines residual imbalance with an outcome contrast, favoring splits that separate outcome-relevant regions where imbalance remains. This couples representation learning with covariate balancing rather than treating balancing as a downstream step. We establish an oracle-type bound that links the iterative construction to weighting error and causal bias. Simulations exhibit improvements in causal estimation relative to existing forest-kernel approaches. Real-data applications illustrate the practical behavior of BGF across observational studies.

papers.title: Observational Test of the Maximum-Entropy Conjecture for Black-Hole Mergers with GW250114
papers.summary: The remnants of binary black-hole (BBH) mergers are accurately described by numerical relativity, but the physical principle governing the selection of the final states remains unclear. A recently proposed maximum-entropy conjecture suggests that a BBH merger produces the Kerr BH that maximizes the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, subject to the post-Newtonian formalism or balance laws for energy and angular momentum. In this work, we test this conjecture with the event GW250114, inferring the progenitor and remnant properties from the observed pre-merge and post-merge signals, separately. We construct the surrogate Kerr entropy associated with candidate remnant states along the inferred energy-angular-momentum trajectory. We then compare the maximum-entropy state with the independently inferred mass and dimensionless spin of the final BH. We find that the conjecture predicts a remnant mass of $M_f=70.0^{+0.35}_{-0.21}\,M_\odot$ and spin of $χ_f=0.70^{+0.00}_{-0.01}$, compared with the ringdown estimates $M_f={72.3}^{+3.6}_{-3.7}\,M_\odot$ and $χ_f=0.74^{+0.05}_{-0.07}$. The entropy deviation is consistent with zero within the $68\%$ credible interval for our fiducial analysis, and variations in the pre-merger truncation time and quasi-normal modes (QNM) content reveal no compelling discrepancy with the conjecture.

papers.title: The potential impact of fiscal rule changes on digital products trade
papers.summary: The WTO moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions lapsed in March 2026, allowing governments to impose tariffs on cross-border digital products, alongside other instruments such as digital services taxes (DSTs). Yet, how tariffs and DSTs compare in the revenue they raise and their effect on trade in digital products has not yet been assessed. Here we combine bilateral trade in 31 digital product categories in 2016-2024 with DST rates and tariffs on physical analogues, estimate gravity models and simulate alternative fiscal regimes. We find that digital trade is lower in destinations with a DST, but within destinations it declines only temporarily after adoption. In conditional scenarios for 2024 based on the event study estimate, adding tariff equivalents to DSTs raises revenue from USD 2.7 to 6.9 billion and lowers trade by about 1.4%, and replacing DSTs with tariff equivalents raises USD 4.3 billion. We also find that tariff-equivalent payments are attributed mainly to the United States and DST payments to subsidiary locations such as Ireland. In sum, these results suggest that tariffs on digital products could raise more revenue than DSTs at a modest cost in trade.

papers.title: Inventory and Assortment Optimization under General Choice: A Unified Approximation Framework
papers.summary: We study joint inventory and assortment optimization under general substitutable choice models. Before a selling horizon, a decision maker chooses initial inventories subject to a capacity constraint on total units stocked, and customers then arrive sequentially and choose among the offered products. We consider two settings, show-all inventory selection, in which every in-stock product must be offered, and dynamic assortment personalization, in which the decision maker observes each customer's type and may adapt the offered assortment to remaining inventory and purchase history. We develop a unified framework linking each setting to a static optimization problem. For show-all inventory selection, a polynomial-time $α$-approximation for cardinality-constrained static assortment optimization yields guarantees of $0.486α$ under deterministic or Poisson arrivals and $0.4328α$ under increasing-failure-rate (IFR) arrivals. For personalization, the same guarantees hold when $α$ is the approximation factor for the joint assortment and customization problem of El Housni and Topaloglu. Our approach combines a fluid relaxation, demand-dependent fractional inventory allocations, bounds on expected truncated demand, and dependent rounding. Notably, our personalized policy fixes one assortment per customer type before the horizon and then offers every in-stock product within it, so it requires no dynamic re-optimization despite competing against the optimal fully adaptive policy. Finally, we construct instances in which optimal show-all revenue approaches only one-half of the fluid bound under deterministic arrivals and $1-w\approx0.4328567$ under IFR arrivals, where $we^w=1$. With an exact static assortment oracle, our IFR guarantee approaches the latter factor arbitrarily closely.

papers.title: Neural networks and games
papers.summary: Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.

papers.title: Iterated Elimination of Dominated Mixed Strategies
papers.summary: This note compares two iterated dominance procedures, one based on eliminating mixed strategies and one based on eliminating pure strategies. It shows that, in compact and continuous games, the mixed-strategy procedure can trail the pure-strategy procedure by at most one round: If the pure-strategy procedure terminates at round $M$, the mixed-strategy procedure terminates at either $M$ or $M+1$, and this bound is tight. It also provides two characterizations of the mixed-strategy procedure that are round-for-round equivalent to it and that require checking for improvements only against opponents' pure strategies.

papers.title: TACT: A Pragmatic Approach to Qualitative Analysis with an AI Council
papers.summary: Qualitative data can tell software teams what their stakeholders need, yet rigorously analyzing thousands of qualitative responses takes expert time that few teams can afford or justify. Teams therefore often face a false choice: leave the responses unanalyzed, or hand them to a large language model and accept its interpretation and judgment. In this paper, we take a pragmatic approach to AI-assisted qualitative analysis and present TACT (Traceable AI Council for Thematic analysis), a procedure that enables such analysis at scale while keeping teams in control of interpretation and judgment. TACT comes in two variants: TACT-Lite, the core AI council procedure, and TACT-Full, which adds adversaries (models from other model families that critique each model's output) and a decision model that surfaces high-uncertainty code assignments. We evaluated TACT on an independent dataset of 256 Stack Overflow threads qualitatively coded by other researchers. Against their labels, TACT's candidate codebook achieved an F1 of 0.75-0.77 and its final coding an F1 of 0.71-0.72. On a held-out sample, agreement between our own manual coding and TACT's coding was Cohen's $κ$ of 0.79-0.85. TACT is also economical: model calls cost \$13.77 (TACT-Lite) to \$33.59 (TACT-Full) per 100 threads. Finally, drawing on our experience building and validating TACT, we identify pitfalls in AI-assisted qualitative analysis, describe safeguards to address them, and offer guidance for teams and researchers applying TACT in practice.

papers.title: Learning to Design Information
papers.summary: Information designers, such as large language models and online platforms, often do not know the subjective beliefs of their receivers or users. We construct learning algorithms enabling the designer to learn the belief of a strategic receiver through repeated interactions. Our learning algorithms are robust to the receiver's strategic manipulation of the learning process of the designer. We study regret relative to two benchmarks to measure the performance of the algorithms. The static benchmark is $T$ times the single-period optimum for the designer under a known belief. The dynamic benchmark, which is stronger, characterizes global dynamic optimality for the designer under a known belief. Our learning algorithms allow the designer to achieve no regret against both benchmarks at fast convergence speeds of $O(\frac{\log^2 T}{T})$, significantly faster than other approaches in the literature.
papers.comment: 85 pages, 4 figures, 2 figures drawn in latex

papers.title: A General Theory of Dynamic Mechanism Design with Endogenous Information and Hidden Actions
papers.summary: We develop a general theory of dynamic mechanism design along two dimensions: joint endogeneity and interaction of hidden actions, information production, and disclosure; and generality across economic environments and feasibility structures. We accommodate correlated private information, interdependent preferences, and potentially infinite-dimensional allocations. We introduce joint perfect correlated Bayesian equilibrium, establish a dynamic revelation principle under this concept, and recursively characterize incentive compatibility. Focusing on a private-values environment allows us to characterize joint incentives through choice optimality, reporting-envelope first-order conditions, global integral monotonicity, and history-report incentives. We derive an exact dynamic information-rent identity, conditional revenue equivalence, and dynamic virtual surplus. Comparing first-best, two second-best, and third-best contracts distinguishes information rents, hidden-action implementation costs, and direct information-production expenditures, revealing nonadditive interactions and branched outcomes. We characterize feasible and optimal disclosure. Applications show the Milgrom-Weber revenue ranking can reverse with endogenous information acquisition, while optimal financial-contract disclosure may be absent, interior, or complete.

papers.title: Efficient Gaussian Process Modeling for Large Replicated and Censored Data in Industrial Research
papers.summary: Gaussian process regression is widely used for modeling responses in both physical and computer experiments. In practice, data from physical experiments may include replications and be subject to censoring due to equipment limitations or contextual constraints, and such datasets can be large, posing a scalability challenge for standard Gaussian process inference. Motivated by a real-world industrial research study, we develop a Gaussian process modeling framework that efficiently analyzes large replicated and censored data. Our approach integrates a Vecchia approximation for computational scalability with a likelihood-based formulation that fully exploits replication and rigorously incorporates information from censored observations, analogous to exact simulation from truncated distributions. Through experiments on synthetic data and a real case study from industrial research, we demonstrate that the proposed method yields improved predictive accuracy and reliable uncertainty quantification compared to existing approaches, making it well suited for large-scale applications with structured replication and incomplete data.

papers.title: High-dimensional Four-Level Structured Functional Principal Component Analysis for Unbalanced Level Data with Application to Concussion Data
papers.summary: We implement the Structured Functional Principal Component Analysis (SFPCA) framework of Shou et al. (2015) in a four-level nested setting with arbitrarily unbalanced group sizes at every level of the hierarchy. While the SFPCA framework can in principle accommodate deeper hierarchical structures, practical implementations remain challenging when the number of curves is large and the hierarchy is highly unbalanced. Our contributions are twofold. First, we operationalize SFPCA for four hierarchical levels with arbitrary unbalancedness across units. Second, we propose a memory-efficient computational strategy that makes the analysis of large collections of curves feasible on conventional hardware. In particular, we construct the four design-specific matrices required for the Method of Moments (MoM) estimators of the level-specific covariance operators while controlling their memory footprint, which would otherwise grow prohibitively with the number of curves. We illustrate the approach using three subsets of the NCAA-DoD Grand Alliance Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium dataset (2014-2017).

papers.title: Bumblebee radiation from neutral matter around a black hole
papers.summary: We investigate bumblebee radiation generated by neutral matter orbiting a black hole with a radial spacelike vector vacuum. Starting from a point particle coupled minimally to the metric, we derive the curvature induced vector current and the potential response required by its conservation. For a localized circular source with no independent radial boundary current, this response gives $δV'=ξρ/4$. The axial vector source instead follows the radial transport of angular momentum and vanishes for circular motion. A slightly eccentric orbit excites an axial dipole at the orbital frequency $Ω$ and a quadrupole contribution at $2Ω$, with outgoing amplitudes proportional to $ev^3$ and $ev^4$, respectively, where $v=\sqrt{M/a}$. We construct their retarded response and obtain the leading coefficients through weak field matching. Reconstruction of the observer's tidal tensor gives the dipole strain $h_{\hat r\hatφ}^{V,10}=ξ^2b^2μev^3\sinθ\cos[Ω(t-R)]/(8πR)$. The corresponding partial luminosity is $P_{B,10}^{\infty}=ξ^2b^2μ^2e^2v^{12}/(48πM^2)$ at the leading order. Remarkably, the ordinary neutral matter produces an additional radial transverse tidal signal even when the homogeneous gravitational master operator remains in Schwarzschild form.
papers.comment: 12 pages in double column and 5 figures

papers.title: How Do Artificial Agents Make Decisions in Light of Visual Data?
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated significant advances in reasoning with visual data, which is particularly important given that much of human knowledge is encoded visually in scientific articles and other sources. However, a gap remains in understanding how artificial agents, powered by VLMs, perceive and navigate decision-making under uncertainty in the presence of visual data. This study explores this gap by evaluating and analyzing autonomous decision-making processes. Building upon prior work in visualization literacy and decision theory, we conducted two complementary studies: one examining how agents perceive and quantify uncertainty encoded in visualizations, and another investigating how artificial agents make decisions based on visual data in the form of images. We analyzed perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization types. Our results show that GPT-4o demonstrates the highest accuracy in perceiving uncertainty in pie and bar charts among the tested models. For decision-making, autonomous agents showed the best alignment with rational decision theory when uncertainty was represented through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.
papers.comment: Presented at the Workshop on GenAI, Agents, and the Future of VIS, held in conjunction with IEEE VIS, 2026

papers.title: Bayesian Superpopulation Models for Population-Based Diabetes Surveillance Using Multi-Site Electronic Health Record Data
papers.summary: Electronic health records (EHRs) are increasingly used for disease surveillance. However, data collected in EHRs may not be a representative sample of the target population for inference. Methods for EHR-based surveillance remain in their nascence. In addition to simple weighting approaches, researchers have used multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP), a popular technique for finite population quantity estimation that remains understudied in EHRs. We are motivated by a US-based collaborative to modernize diabetes surveillance using EHR data from different health system centers across the country. To estimate type 1 diabetes (T1D) prevalence in children and adolescents, we propose and evaluate three Bayesian superpopulation models that are distinguished by how they account for two important features of EHR data: unobserved heterogeneity and data sparsity. The three models include an analysis of variance-inspired approach; a model with geographic effects varying by demographic subgroup; and MRP, which we consider as the reference model. We apply the models to estimate prevalence overall and in demographic- and geographic-based subgroups. Using plasmode simulations, we evaluate model estimation performance while preserving the complexity of the EHR data. Our results show that the superpopulation-based prevalence estimates were higher than those observed in the EHR sample alone, with the magnitude of the differences varying by health system center. The bias and coverage probabilities of MRP markedly worsened when the EHR sample size was smaller or the selection mechanism was more complex. Overall, the superpopulation model based on analysis of variance demonstrated the best estimation performance.

papers.title: Predictability over Volatility: When simple strategies help households save on fuel
papers.summary: What reasonable strategies can households use to save on gasoline or diesel purchases under different pricing functions? We assess basic strategies households might employ under a simplified model of a 10-gallon tank, fixed fuel consumption between refill opportunities, and price changes at each opportunity to refill. Purchases always fill the tank, and if the tank is empty, it must be refilled regardless of price. We explore three strategy types: price-independent (filling once the tank is below a specific level), price-dependent (filling when the price is below the last $n$ days or their average), and mixed (filling only below a set level, and then only when the price is below the last $n$ days or their average). We construct price functions from the nearest-in-time US weekly averages of regular gasoline and diesel, filling in higher-frequency values with a smoothing spline, linear interpolation, and random draws from normal and uniform distributions based on national averages. Additional simulations are built using Brownian motion. Together, these pricing models span a wide range of volatilities. We find that price-independent strategies are effective for the spline and linear functions, which have low volatility, while price-dependent strategies are effective for the normal and uniform distributions, which are highly volatile. Brownian motion, despite its mid-range volatility, admits no effective strategy. Our findings suggest that the predictability of price movements, whether prices trend or revert toward a stable level, matters more for household strategies than overall volatility: the random walk is volatile in the middle of our range yet offers households no usable signal. Policymakers can therefore assist households by addressing how prices move from day to day, not only the retail prices they face.

papers.title: On the Theory of Multidimensional Stationary Random Processes (1941): Translation and Commentary
papers.summary: This edition provides an English translation and commentary on V. N. Zasukhin's 1941 note "On the Theory of Multidimensional Stationary Random Processes," originally published in Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR, 33(7-8), 435-437. The note states a multivariate extension of Wold's decomposition: an orthogonal decomposition into singular and regular components, a one-sided moving-average representation of the regular component in terms of orthonormal innovation sequences, and a spectral criterion for regularity of full rank. The latter combines absolute continuity of the spectral functions with positivity and logarithmic integrability of the determinant of the spectral density matrix. Whittle (1953) explicitly credited Zasukhin with the multivariate generalization. The original results are presented without detailed proofs. A separate editorial note discusses their historical reception and explains the terminology. A retypeset Russian transcription is included for comparison.

papers.title: Economic Policy Uncertainty Index for Poland: Data, Construction, and Validation
papers.summary: We construct a continuous monthly Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index for Poland spanning January 2000 to June 2026, following the newspaper-based Baker-Bloom-Davis (BBD) methodology. The index uses six deep-history Polish newspapers (Rzeczpospolita, Parkiet, Gazeta Wyborcza, Dziennik Gazeta Prawna, Gazeta Polska Codziennie, and Puls Biznesu), scaled by article volume, standardized to unit standard deviation over a fixed 2000-2024 baseline (300 months), averaged across available papers each period, and normalized so the baseline mean equals 100. Because newspapers enter the panel at different dates, a naive expanding-panel average can jump at each entry point from a change in composition rather than real uncertainty. We correct for this using the BBD Appendix A splicing procedure: a backward chain-splice from the richest six-paper anchor panel that matches dispersion via a multiplicative scale factor and matches level via a multiplicative ratio over each overlap window, yielding an index that is level-continuous across all entry points. The index rises sharply during the COVID-19 lockdown, the 2022 energy crisis, and the 2023 change of government, with its largest reaction following the 2016 Brexit referendum -- an external event with major implications for Poland's economic-policy environment. In month-on-month changes, Poland's EPU is moderately correlated with the US (0.26) and global (0.25) EPU indices. Together with the event-based evidence, these modest correlations support our central finding: EPU Index PL captures economic policy uncertainty that is predominantly domestic, driven mainly by developments in Poland's own economic policy rather than merely international spillovers, though international shocks remain relevant insofar as they create uncertainty about Poland's own policy decisions.
papers.comment: 45 pages, 4 figures. JEL: D80, E32, E66, G18, L50. EPU Index Poland Working Paper No. 01/2026. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/EP759

papers.title: Contextual Pictograms for Repairing Multilingual ASR Errors
papers.summary: Speech transcription errors can be difficult to recognize when competing word hypotheses are unfamiliar or visually similar. We describe an interface that combines alternative transcripts, replay and contextually checked pictograms for selected uncertain concepts. The system will initially support French and Spanish functional utterances. A counterbalanced study will assess whether pictorial feedback helps listeners recover the speaker's intended action beyond text alternatives alone. We will also quantify semantic mismatch and additional interaction time, since an inappropriate image can reinforce the wrong interpretation rather than repair it.

papers.title: Proton generalized parton distributions from electromagnetic form factors: A theoretically constrained phenomenological reconstruction
papers.summary: We present a theoretically constrained phenomenological reconstruction of the unpolarized, chiral-even, leading-twist proton generalized parton distributions $H^q$ and $E^q$. At zero skewness, valence-quark distributions are combined with flavor-dependent exponential profiles calibrated simultaneously against phenomenological representations of the proton and neutron electromagnetic form factors. The construction imposes exact valence and anomalous-magnetic-moment normalizations, the low-scale condition $B^{u+d}(0)=0$, the required endpoint behavior, and the complete Gaussian impact-parameter positivity bound. The resulting parametrization provides a reasonable description of the electromagnetic form factors and their slopes while revealing the tension between strict GPD consistency and a precision reproduction of all low-$Q^2$ observables within the adopted ansatz. We extend the distributions to nonzero skewness using normalized double distributions and introduce an independent $D$-term to complete the relevant Mellin polynomials. We examine electromagnetic and energy--momentum-tensor form factors, impact-parameter distributions, positivity, polynomiality, and illustrative mechanical properties. The analysis distinguishes information constrained by electromagnetic data from additional assumptions governing skewness and the mechanical sector, thereby providing a transparent elastic baseline for future studies of nucleon-to-resonance transition GPDs.

papers.title: Geodesic completeness and photon propagation in a superconducting T-duality black hole
papers.summary: The purpose of this article is twofold. First, we study the geodesic completeness of the string T-duality black hole with the Raychaudhuri equation, for radial massive particles of arbitrary specific energy $\varepsilon$. Exact proper-time quadratures reveal three classes of observers: supercritical observers reach the regular centre in finite proper time through a caustic and pass through it, critical observers ($\varepsilon=1$) approach it only asymptotically with finite expansion, and subcritical observers are reflected at a fold caustic. Because the lapse is analytic and even in $r$, geodesics continue regularly through the centre, and all three classes are complete on the stipulated maximal extension. A diverging expansion therefore signals a caustic of the congruence rather than an endpoint of the geodesics, in contrast with Schwarzschild spacetime. Second, radial Maxwell rays are likewise complete but form a single class, since a massless ray carries no energy scale. We propose to model the black-hole core itself as a superconductor, with London response $μ^2=4πκρ$ attributed to the existing source. A symmetry-breaking potential with a vacuum-energy offset reproduces the de Sitter core and its photon mass exactly at the centre and approximately in the inner core; since no static scalar theory reproduces the anisotropic source further out, the full radial response remains phenomenological. The resulting Hamiltonian rays follow timelike geodesics of $μ^2g_{μν}$ up to reparametrisation and reproduce the three classes, separated by the central mass $μ_0$, while the density gradient of the core adds a defocusing contribution near the centre. We also distinguish Hamiltonian completeness from completeness of the conformal metric.
papers.comment: 17 pages, no figures. Comments are welcome

papers.title: Personalized Visual Support After Automatic Speech Recognition
papers.summary: Many spoken-language interfaces stop at producing a transcript. This project examines how a second layer of optional text and pictorial support can be adapted to individual needs. We specify four presentation levels and a behavior-based selection policy driven by replay requests, response latency and recent comprehension. After expert review of the mappings, we will compare fixed and adaptive presentation using counterbalanced spoken instructions. The study is designed to measure comprehension, usability and which modality listeners rely on, not to claim that transcript embellishment uniformly benefits listeners.

papers.title: Complex phase diagram and thermodynamic supercriticality of five-dimensional four-charge AdS black holes in $STU-W^2U$ gauged supergravity
papers.summary: In this paper, we investigate the complex phase structure and thermodynamic supercriticality of static four-charge anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes in five-dimensional $STU-W^2U$ gauged supergravity, with all four physical electric charges held fixed. A Van der Waals-like first-order small/large black hole phase transition is found to terminate at a critical point. By analytically continuing the fixed-charge thermodynamic relations, we trace the two real spinodal singularities through criticality into a complex-conjugate pair in the supercritical region. The corresponding spinodal temperatures exhibit the characteristic $3/2$ near-critical scaling, connecting the subcritical temperature splitting with the imaginary parts of the supercritical complex temperatures. We construct the associated complex phase diagram and identify a Widom-type crossover line from the real-temperature projection of the complex spinodals. This line progressively deviates from the locus of real heat-capacity maxima as the pressure increases. At higher pressures, the real heat-capacity extrema eventually merge and disappear, while the complex spinodal singularities persist. Together, these results reveal a continuous connection between critical phase transitions and supercritical thermodynamics through complex singularity structures, providing further insight into the thermodynamic phase behavior of multicharge supergravity black holes.

papers.title: Debiased Conditional Independence Tests for Causal Effects
papers.summary: We propose robust tests for causal effects on potentially high-dimensional outcomes where there may be selection into treatment. These tests measure conditional independence of outcomes from treatment assignment by asking whether treatment can be predicted from outcomes more accurately than from covariates alone. We design three such tests of conditional independence. First, we propose a conditional randomization test based on an inverse propensity weighted mean squared error test statistic. If the propensity score is known, the test controls size in finite samples. Second, we propose a double-residualization approach, where we partial out covariate effects from both treatment and outcome-based treatment predictions, and test whether the correlation between the residuals is zero. Third, we propose a test based on an augmented inverse propensity weighted estimator built around doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal population moments that are necessary and sufficient for conditional independence. Simulations show that all three tests improve power over a joint Wald test based on a seemingly unrelated regression across many non-linear settings, particularly under heavy tails, outliers, mixtures, heterogeneous effects, and effects with opposite signs.

papers.title: Transport along Local Annealing Paths: Wasserstein Geometry and Multimodal Sampling
papers.summary: Variational approaches to learning transport maps for multimodal sampling can suffer from mode collapse. One way to mitigate this problem is to learn transport along a prescribed path of intermediate distributions defined by geometric annealing. We show that annealing can take a substantial detour in Wasserstein space: when mass moves between modes, the path can be much longer than the distance between its endpoints. We further link path geometry to transport learning, showing that long annealing paths can slow population optimization, while sufficiently regular paths permit rapid convergence. Motivated by these findings, we propose componentwise annealed transport (CAT) to reduce the need for mass transfer between modes. Starting from a mode-informed mixture reference, CAT constructs an exact mixture decomposition of the target and learns separate transport maps along componentwise annealing paths. We estimate the component weights separately and show that these estimates remain consistent even when the learned flows are inexact. We also develop adaptive annealing schedules guided by transport effort. Experiments on multimodal synthetic distributions and Bayesian inference problems demonstrate improvements in transport learning and sampling efficiency.

papers.title: Geometric ergodicity of the block Gibbs sampler for Bayesian linear mixed models with scale mixtures of normal random effects
papers.summary: We study a Bayesian linear mixed model whose random effects follow a scale mixture of normal distributions with an arbitrary mixing distribution, a class that contains the Student-t, slash, contaminated normal, normal-generalized inverse Gaussian and Laplace laws. Conditionally conjugate priors lead to a three-block Gibbs sampler that alternates between the variance components, the latent precision weights, and the regression coefficients together with the random effects. Using a drift function built from fractional powers, we give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity of this chain, which involve a moment of the mixing distribution of some order larger than 1/2 and its behaviour near the origin. An equivariance of the sampler under rescaling of the design then shows that the conditions hold for all the families above, including Student-t random effects with any degrees of freedom, for every random-effects design matrix, full rank or not, with the rank entering only the conditions on the priors of the variance components. Together with posterior moment bounds, geometric ergodicity justifies Monte Carlo standard errors and effective-sample-size stopping rules for the regression coefficients and the log-variance components. Simulations examine these procedures at practical run lengths: joint confidence regions need a correction for the number of batches, and under sequential stopping their observed coverage remains slightly below the nominal level. We illustrate the methods with longitudinal beta-HCG measurements from early pregnancies, in which the latent weights reveal larger between-subject variability among abnormal pregnancies.

papers.title: Sensitivity Analysis in Population Shares
papers.summary: Empirical work often relies on assumptions on the distribution of random variables, such as potential outcomes or latent variables, to identify some parameter of interest. We introduce a unified framework for assessing the sensitivity of a target estimand to relaxing these distributional assumptions for a given share of the population. We derive bounds on the values the estimand can take as this share varies between 0 and 1, and compute the bounds using tractable finite-dimensional programs. We propose plug-in estimators for the bounds and characterize their large sample properties. We also show that our bounds recover exact nonparametric sharp bounds at no additional computational cost, and introduce summary measures that separate misspecification uncertainty from sampling uncertainty and rank studies by their robustness. We apply our framework to assess the robustness of (i) average treatment effects in randomized experiments with attrition, (ii) counterfactual predictions in structural models, and (iii) formula instruments. We provide R and Python packages implementing all our methods.
