papers.title: A covariance density for a point process and a random field
papers.summary: The spatial point process literature offers a well-developed theory for characterizing covariances within a point process or between different point processes using joint intensity functions or cross joint intensity functions. However, similar summary statistics are missing for characterizing the covariance between a point process and a random field. We introduce a normalized mixed covariance density that fills this gap for covariances between variables of a random field and linear functionals of a point process. We construct a non-parametric kernel estimator of the covariance density and a data-driven method for bandwidth selection. We further use our estimate of the covariance density to test the dependence between a point process and a random field. Several existing tests require observations of the random field at the events of the point process. These are often not available when the random field is sampled on a grid unrelated to the point process. Then interpolation is needed to impute random field values at point process events. Our covariance density estimate in contrast does not require interpolation. We investigate the performance of our non-parametric estimator and the method for bandwidth selection in applications to simulated and real data.

papers.title: Just the Facts: How Dialogues with AI Reduce Conspiracy Beliefs
papers.summary: Personalized dialogues with AI substantially reduce conspiracy beliefs. To identify why, we conducted two experiments with U.S. adults recruited online (total N = 2,193) that removed possible causes one at a time. The debunking effect was robust to disclosing the AI's persuasive goal, framing the exchange as a debate, instructing the AI to inform rather than persuade, halving its response length, altering how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message. Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially reduced the debunking effect. Content analyses of the AI's output and participants' own accounts linked larger reductions in conspiracy beliefs to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy. AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence. Our results suggest that humans might be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.

papers.title: An obstruction to cosmic acceleration from shift-symmetric dark sector interactions
papers.summary: Using the effective field theory of cosmological media, we show that derivative interactions in the dark sector between a perfect fluid and a superfluid cannot support slow-roll expansion while remaining free from instabilities. Furthermore, decomposing the dark sector medium into effective dark matter and dark energy components, we find that the stability conditions exclude a phantom-to-non-phantom crossing. Our approach gives a clear route for constructing theoretically viable dark sector models, and highlights the fundamental constraints that stability requirements impose on their cosmological dynamics.

papers.title: Decision Models as Scalable Economic Surrogates that Capture Human Variation
papers.summary: Decision Models (DMs), a new class of AI models, give fast responses and return a probability distribution over a fixed set of options. These properties make them candidate human surrogates in economic simulations and surveys, a role increasingly filled by Large Language Models (LLMs), which are costly at scale and under-represent the variation in human behaviour. We present a first evaluation of DMs as human surrogates in economics, comparing 10 DMs with 8 LLMs in three economic settings: a household spending survey on consumption, several classic economic games and a labour-market field experiment. Frontier DMs, those that score highest on general decision-making benchmarks, reproduce the variation in human responses more closely than LLMs in all three settings. They capture the modal human response as well as LLMs in the spending survey, but less well in the economic games. Frontier DMs are also roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and can be over a hundred times cheaper. Together, these results suggest that DMs capture the heterogeneity of human behaviour better than LLMs and make large-scale economic simulations more feasible.

papers.title: Whose Transparency is it Anyway? Understanding Generative AI Transparency Needs and Gaps Across Stakeholders
papers.summary: Transparency has become a central principle in AI governance, yet there is little agreement about what transparency means, for whom, and in what contexts. Drawing on interpretive flexibility within the Social Construction of Technology, this paper examines how different stakeholders understand and experience transparency in generative AI. This study draws from a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders, and policymakers, complemented by a structured focus group with end-users, grounding the quantitative findings in qualitative insights from the group most underserved by current transparency practice. We present three key findings. First, all three groups share similar understandings of what transparency means and what it should afford, centered on ensuring accuracy and privacy. Second, gaps between the importance of transparency features and their perceived availability are substantially larger for end-users than builders, revealing how power shapes what gets built and who it serves. Only 28% of end-users report that current transparency practices reflect their needs very well, compared to 53% of builders and 49% of policymakers. Third, transparency is situationally constructed, priorities shift with context and task structure, with role-specific frames activating when context demands them and receding when it does not. We argue that meaningful AI transparency requires moving beyond a one-size-fits-all solution, including current emphases on AI disclosure and static documentation, toward pluralistic transparency infrastructures that reflect the needs of diverse users and stakeholders.

papers.title: Raychaudhuri-Ehlers Kinematics on Quantum State-Space: Caustics and Extrinsic Quantum Geometry
papers.summary: Quantum mechanics is inherently geometric in that the pure states form a curved complex manifold and the Schrödinger evolution defines a Hamiltonian flow on this space. Geometry identifies constraints on flows on quantum state-space that hold independently of their microscopic realization. We uncover such universal behavior in families of geodesic paths on the quantum state-space using the Raychaudhuri-Ehlers equations. We show that the complex structure leads to tidal anisotropy in the curvature, and for Hilbert space dimension $N\geq3$, complete point-emitted geodesic bundles necessarily develop shear and undergo direction-selective focusing at finite distance. We give these geometric results an information-theoretic interpretation in terms of fidelity susceptibility and quantum Fisher information. For ground-state manifolds constrained by physical parameters, we resolve the tidal curvature into Berry-curvature-dependent ambient tides and contributions from extrinsic bending within the full ambient state space. We further relate extrinsic bending to variations in the unitary generator of motion along intrinsic geodesics. We present exact many-body geometric results for the transverse-field XY spin chain. The product structure of the ground state leads to an exact cancellation of the ambient tide, including its Berry-curvature enhancement, by extrinsic curvature contributions. At the zero-field Ising point, we obtain exact results at finite size and show that the shear source for anisotropy-directed motion is entirely extrinsic relative to the full many-body state-space. For the metric in the thermodynamic limit, the geodesic families exhibit repeated $A_2$ fold catastrophes inside the ferromagnetic phase. Our framework thus separates universal state-space effects from those of physical restrictions and exposes their consequences in a paradigmatic many-body system.

papers.title: Goldstone theory of gluon saturation in high energy QCD: From color glass to color superfluid condensate
papers.summary: In the high energy Regge asymptotics of QCD, the rapid overpopulation of gluons leads to gluon saturation, characterized by nonperturbative semi-classical lumpy configurations of size $1/Q_S$, where $Q_S\gg Λ_{\rm QCD}$ is a dynamical semi-hard saturation scale. We discuss here a generalization of the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) framework describing this phenomenon that is obtained by carefully treating the breaking of global symmetries by the condensate. In particular, we show that the breaking of a global subgroup of color results in a Goldstone effective field theory (EFT) whose dynamics is characterized by a Goldstone decay constant $f_G = \sqrt{N} Q_S$, where $N=O(1/α_S)$ is the phase space occupancy of the condensate, which is large for $α_S(Q_S)\ll 1$. Further, the coupling of these colored Goldstones to collinear gluon modes leads to a depletion of the condensate, thereby modifying the static shockwave scattering framework of the CGC on timescales controlled by $f_G$. The CGC EFT on these longer time scales is a novel color superfluid. Low frequency modes with $ω\leq α_S Q_S$ in an external probe of the CGC are sensitive to superfluid dynamics, with interesting physical consequences for deeply inelastic scattering and ultrarelativistic nuclear collisions.

papers.title: Search for the 229Pa Parity Doublet via Internal-Conversion Spectroscopy at FRIB
papers.summary: The radioisotope $^{229}$Pa is predicted to possess a nearly degenerate ground-state parity doublet. Previous $γ$-ray and conversion-electron spectroscopy suggests a splitting of $ΔE = (60\pm 50)~\mathrm{eV}$, although the doublet's existence remains unconfirmed. Such a small splitting would give $^{229}$Pa an exceptionally large enhancement of symmetry-violating nuclear properties. However, the splitting, and with it the sensitivity of $^{229}$Pa to CP-violating physics, remains uncertain by orders of magnitude. We propose an experiment to measure this splitting with sub-eV precision within a few days of measurement time by using delayed-coincidence internal-conversion spectroscopy of $^{229}$Pa ions produced by the electron-capture decay of $^{229}$U$^{+}$ ions stored in a Penning trap at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams (FRIB). This measurement would provide the key nuclear-structure input needed to establish $^{229}$Pa as a leading candidate for next-generation atomic and molecular electric-dipole-moment (EDM) experiments.

papers.title: Quantum computing for high energy nuclear physics
papers.summary: Quantum information science (QIS) offers a new set of conceptual and computational tools ideally suited to exploring the many-body, out-of-equilibrium, and real-time properties of strongly interacting quantum systems. These themes find a natural counterpart in high energy nuclear physics, whose central goal is to describe the properties of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the theory of the strong interaction, under extreme conditions. Relevant examples range from the formation and internal structure of hadrons, to the collective and thermalization dynamics of strongly interacting QCD matter, and the properties of complex many-body scattering processes. Although tremendous progress has been made over the past decades in our understanding of QCD in the nuclear physics context, through perturbative methods, lattice QCD, and effective theory descriptions, phenomena that are intrinsically connected to real-time dynamics, highly entangled many-body evolution, or finite density regimes remain only partially accessible with existing approaches. In this article, we argue that QIS can help realize a new paradigm for addressing these open questions. With the aim of making the discussion accessible to both high energy nuclear physics and QIS audiences, we provide an overview of selected open problems in high energy nuclear physics, with emphasis on aspects motivated by collider phenomenology, and discuss how they can be approached using QIS tools. This connection is illustrated through representative examples drawn from the recent literature, making the case that QIS can become a driving force for discovery in nuclear physics in the coming years.
papers.comment: 47 pages, 17 figures, Contribution to Encyclopedia of Nuclear Physics, comments are welcomed

papers.title: Black hole quasinormal mode excitation and mixing for coupled fields
papers.summary: The idea of testing the nature of black holes and possible deviations from general relativity from their oscillation spectrum, known as ``black hole spectroscopy'', has become an experimental science. In many modified theories of gravity, the gravitational perturbations couple to additional degrees of freedom, leading to mode mixing and to a more complex ringdown signal. We adopt the parametrized quasinormal mode formalism for nonrotating black holes to study coupled perturbations in modified gravity theories in order to understand how the interaction with additional fields affects the quasinormal mode frequencies and their amplitudes. We compute the quasinormal mode spectrum of the coupled system in the frequency domain using direct integration and a matrix-valued continued-fraction method. We then compare the results with time-domain evolutions, where we extract the mode frequencies and amplitudes using the Prony method as well as least-squares fitting. In the weak-coupling regime, the scaling of the amplitudes associated with the gravitational-led and secondary-led modes can be understood perturbatively. The excitation of additional families of ringdown modes can become significant even when the frequency shifts remain moderate. We use our numerical time evolutions to provide ready-to-use coefficients for the mode amplitudes for representative initial data configurations. We work out specific examples, including dynamical Chern-Simons gravity and the special near-resonant case of coupled perturbations between the polar and axial quasinormal modes. Our theory-agnostic characterization of coupled systems should be useful to quantify systematic effects in black hole spectroscopy with next-generation gravitational-wave detectors.

papers.title: The quasi-topological space of quasi-topological gravities
papers.summary: We investigate general properties of quasi-topological theories of gravity involving infinite towers of polynomial densities and of their regular vacuum black hole solutions. We show that every positive-mass regular vacuum solution necessarily possesses a de Sitter core, while Minkowski and anti-de Sitter cores are excluded. Regarding the horizon structure, we prove that asymptotically flat and anti-de Sitter regular black holes always admit extremal configurations. We find that there is no upper bound on the number of horizons and that horizons of arbitrarily high degeneracy can arise. These results extend to more general theories of gravity with second-order equations on spherically symmetric backgrounds. Finally, we characterize the space of quasi-topological theories admitting regular black holes, showing that it is contractible (in particular, path-connected and simply connected) and that regularity is stable under suitably small deformations of the higher-order couplings. In the sense of Spanier, this space is naturally a contractible \emph{quasi-topological} space. Additionally, we prove that any theory defined by a set of couplings up to any arbitrarily high, but finite, curvature order can be completed into a theory yielding regular black hole solutions, while preserving the same set of lower-order couplings. These results show that regular solutions arise in a broad class of quasi-topological gravities and do not require fine-tuning of the couplings.

papers.title: Toward a Quantum Information Foundation for Neutron Scattering
papers.summary: Neutron scattering is a central probe of quantum materials, yet what quantum information can, in principle, be extracted from a scattering experiment remains unclear. Here we formulate neutron scattering as a quantum measurement, with the scattering amplitudes acting as Kraus operators on the material state. This provides a unified description of conventional intensity, coherent scattering, interferometric measurements, and entanglement witnesses, including those based on quantum Fisher information. We then ask how far this connection can be extended to nonlinear properties of a quantum state. For two independently prepared samples, we derive the general structure of probe-mediated measurement probabilities and show that, for spin-projection-conserving dynamics, low-order scattering cannot resolve certain many-body coherences required to determine purity. Conversely, an idealized single-spin protocol shows how probe-mediated exchange can access purity when the appropriate two-copy operation is realized. Our results establish a quantum-information description of neutron scattering and delineate the information accessible through conventional and interferometric measurements.

papers.title: A Bayesian Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg Model for Real-Time EEG Phase Estimation
papers.summary: Real-time phase estimation on stimulus-aligned transient EEG is critical for closed-loop neuromodulation systems targeting the theta-band, yet most real-time phase estimation methods have been developed and validated on resting-state, high-fidelity signals in the alpha band. Recent work has pursued deep learning architectures, while individualized classical bandpass filter tuning remains underexplored. This study characterizes the spectral and temporal properties of non-anticipative bandpass filtering and demonstrates the performance gains achieved through individualized tuning. We present a Bayesian-Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg (BOB) model evaluated on EEG recorded during peripheral vibrotactile stimulation of the left median nerve (theta, N=20 healthy subjects) and on resting-state recordings from the Max Planck Institute's LEMON dataset (alpha, N=20 healthy subjects). BOB was benchmarked against the Deep Dual-Branch Complex Neural Network (DBCNN), EEG Phase Prediction Network (EPN), Phastimate, and Phase Estimation with Autoregressive Padding (PEAP) under matched testing conditions: channel selection, individualized optimization, evaluation time points, and an offline reference phase obtained through zero-phase filtering and the Hilbert transform. Under these testing conditions, BOB achieved matched or better performance than these models at a fraction of the calibration time.

papers.title: Deconfinement Confined to the Heaviest Neutron Stars: Strange Quark Matter from a Flavor-Dressed Contact Interaction
papers.summary: We study cold, electrically neutral, beta-equilibrated quark matter with u, d, and s quarks described by a symmetry-preserving contact interaction whose parameters are fixed in vacuum. The vector repulsion is varied as a fraction 0 < eta < 3/2 of the scalar coupling, and results are given with and without the flavor dressing of the effective coupling. Pure quark matter is not self-bound in this model, and no value of eta produces a star that reaches two solar masses while satisfying the tidal constraint from GW170817; the heaviest configurations owe their mass to an envelope of constituent quarks. We then construct hybrid stars with a relativistic mean-field hadronic phase fitted to GM1 saturation properties, using both Maxwell and Gibbs constructions and a deconfinement bag shift. Tying deconfinement to chiral restoration and requiring a continuous pressure yields an upper bound on this shift. Within that bound, quark matter appears inside stable stars only for eta < 1/2, never below about 4 n0, and only in stars between 2.2 and 2.35Msun, over a stable mass window of at most 0.02Msun. The vector strength that pure quark stars need to become massive prevents deconfinement in hybrid stars. Radii and tidal deformabilities of intermediate-mass stars are therefore set by the hadronic EoS alone; with the softer SLy4 EoS the transition moves to the maximum-mass configuration itself.

papers.title: Whose Guardrail? User Identity Shapes the Effectiveness of Model Disclaimers in Mitigating LLM Political Persuasion
papers.summary: Politically biased AI can shift users' opinions, yet it remains unclear whether model disclaimers protect against such persuasion. We report a preregistered experiment (N=1,586) examining how disclaimer design and user characteristics shape susceptibility to politically biased AI. We varied whether disclaimers identified political bias versus potential inaccuracies and whether they included an explanation. Participants completed two decision-making tasks with an LLM biased against their political views, with outcomes assessed immediately and one week later. Disclaimers identifying political bias and including an explanation reduced persuasion, but effects varied across contexts and did not persist. Individual differences were more consistent predictors: Republicans were more persuaded and reported higher trust than Democrats across tasks. Similarly, participants who used AI more frequently were also more persuaded, whereas those with greater self-reported AI knowledge were less persuaded. These findings suggest that generic disclaimers are not enough: effective safeguards must account for user heterogeneity and context.

papers.title: Aggregating treatment effects across multiple outcomes
papers.summary: Researchers often aggregate outcomes to estimate treatment effects on abstract concepts, such as "crime" or "wealth." First, I document that principal component analysis (PCA), inverse variance matrix (IVM) weighting, and standardized averaging (SA) are commonly used but have unexpected shortcomings. PCA can assign negative weights, need not maximize precision, depends on an arbitrary sign normalization, and can have nonstandard asymptotics. Unlike SA, IVM can assign negative weights, but neither necessarily maximizes precision. Second, I develop a statistical decision-theoretic approach that uses mean-squared error to choose nonnegative weights while accounting for outcome quality. I revisit a study on social distancing.

papers.title: Left-Digit Bias: Theory and Empirical Evidence from a Tax Salience Experiment
papers.summary: Demand often drops sharply at whole-dollar prices. To explain this phenomenon, known as left-digit bias, we develop a random utility model in which consumers consider a good only if its price is below a heterogeneous attention threshold. Masses of consumers with integer attention thresholds generate demand discontinuities. When a tax is introduced, the model predicts a weaker demand response compared to rational choice for left-digit biased consumers. Using data from a tax experiment, we find that the model matches behavioral moments and partially identify the distribution of willingness to pay relative to thresholds. A weak demand response need not imply a low excess burden of taxation and understanding the specific mechanism is important for welfare analysis.

papers.title: iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior
papers.summary: Antibody affinity maturation is a natural optimization process in which B cells acquire mutations through somatic hypermutation (SHM), undergo selection for improved antigen binding, and iteratively evolve toward higher affinity. Computationally modeling this process requires capturing both biologically plausible mutations and antigen-specific selection. However, existing mutation models do not directly optimize binding, while affinity optimization often neglects realistic mutation trajectories. We introduce iGC (in silico Germinal Centers), a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework for antigen-specific antibody optimization. Stage 1 learns an SHM mutation prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset. Stage 2 initializes an RL policy from this prior and optimizes antigen binding with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the frozen prior. To prevent reward exploitation, including repetitive high-reward substitutions and structurally tolerated framework mutations, we introduce a Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective. RewardNet smooths the affinity landscape, while TaxNet penalizes reward overexploitation, jointly defining a learned meta-reward for policy optimization. We evaluate iGC on mutation prediction, SHM consistency, affinity optimization, and mutation diversity. The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline in mutation-site prediction. Following RL optimization, iGC maintains SHM sequence structure. It also achieves a strong exploration-exploitation balance, yielding competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs. These results demonstrate that iGC integrates biologically plausible mutation generation with antigen-specific affinity selection, providing an in silico framework for iterative antibody affinity maturation.

papers.title: Interpretable Social Network Churn Prediction via Ergodic Markov Chains
papers.summary: Predicting social network churn before it becomes visible in aggregate metrics remains an open challenge, particularly in enterprise settings where heterogeneous usage patterns, sparse data, and deployment constraints preclude standard supervised approaches. We formalize this problem as finite-step engagement projection over contributor-role Markov chains, with a stationary-distribution interpretation for ergodic chains in the long-run limit. For each engagement feature type within a network (e.g., Q&A, communities, articles, etc.), users are classified monthly into four behavioral states and a transition matrix is estimated from six months of history. Six-step propagation yields a label-free projection of the contributor mix; for ergodic chains, the Perron-Frobenius theorem establishes convergence under repeated propagation. Comparing projected future engagement to current engagement produces the Health Ratio, a single score requiring no trained model, no labels, and no infrastructure beyond SQL. Validated across seven rolling prediction windows on 11,500+ tenant-level networks, the Health Ratio achieves mean AUC 0.917 with a 156 times churn-rate gradient across risk tiers, outperforming all single-signal baselines and the growth-adjusted variant previously deployed in production. An ablation study shows that six-step propagation achieves similar churn discrimination to the eigenvector-based score. Deployed on Microsoft Engage since October 2025, the framework powers customer health monitoring and has enabled proactive intervention on at-risk networks before decline becomes visible in traditional metrics.
papers.comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Author manuscript accepted for publication in Microsoft Journal of Applied Research (MSJAR), Volume 23, Article 217

papers.title: Shrinkage prior for implicit generative models
papers.summary: Implicit generative models based on deep neural networks have revolutionized many scientific fields, from weather research to language generation. They successfully model complex random objects arising in real-world problems. In this work, we propose a sample-efficient training mechanism for these models. Our approach leverages regularized inference with shrinkage priors and generalized Bayes. In the large $p$ (parameter dimension) and small $n$ (sample size) setting, sparsity-inducing priors have been successfully used for linear regression when $p \gg n$. However, their application to implicit generative models remains challenging due to the intractability of the likelihood function. To address this, we adapt a scoring rule posterior based on a strictly proper scoring rule, following the generalized Bayes framework. We then propose a block SGMCMC within Gibbs sampling mechanism. This enables efficient exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces by identifying a sparse representation of neural implicit generative models. We demonstrate the performance of our proposed method through experiments on $p \gg n$ linear regression and an application of neural generative models.

papers.title: Elliptic and triangular flow responses in O+O and Ne+Ne collisions from hydrodynamics and kinetic theory
papers.summary: Recent light-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider provide an opportunity to investigate the system-size dependence of hydrodynamization and whether the structure of light nuclei can be extracted from collective flow data. Both objectives require an accurate understanding of how the collision dynamics converts initial-state geometry into final-state momentum anisotropies. To this end, and to assess the impact of the experimental results, we compare simulations of O+O and Ne+Ne collisions in hydrodynamic and kinetic theory simulations across opacities. In both ultracentral and peripheral collisions, Ne+Ne-to-O+O elliptic flow ratios are robust against changes in dynamical description, supporting interpretations of data based on nuclear-geometry-driven effects. Triangular-flow ratios instead show substantially stronger sensitivity to nonequilibrium dynamics.

papers.title: Post-stratified importance sampling
papers.summary: Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: Scalable Bayesian inference for time-discretised Markov jump processes via exchangeable particle Gibbs
papers.summary: Inference in stochastic reaction-network models, such as the susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) epidemic model, is crucial for understanding the dynamics of interacting systems in epidemiology, ecology, and systems biology. These models are typically represented as Markov jump processes (MJPs), with discrete, noisy observations and intractable likelihoods. Particle Markov chain Monte Carlo (PMCMC) offers a natural mechanism for inference on these hidden Markov models, but, even in moderate dimensional state spaces, particle degeneracy typically leads to poor mixing of the PMCMC algorithm. This paper focuses on improving the efficiency of particle Gibbs for inference on reaction networks by addressing the degeneracy problem. Building on recent work on the exchangeable particle Gibbs (xPG) sampler for diffusions, this paper develops a novel version of xPG tailored to discrete-state-space reaction networks, where randomness is driven by Poisson processes rather than Brownian motion. We focus on the $τ$-leap discretisation of the MJPs. The proposed method retains the exchangeability framework of xPG while adapting it to the structural and computational challenges specific to reaction networks. The new method is applied to several examples, including four coupled SEIR models, where it substantially improves mixing efficiency compared with standard particle Gibbs. In this example, xPG improves sample efficiency by more than an order of magnitude relative to standard particle Gibbs, making inference feasible in hours rather than weeks. As part of our tuning strategy, we provide a mechanism for tuning the number of particles that is applicable more generally, to any particle Gibbs algorithm.
papers.comment: 21 pages + 19 pages appendix. 6 figures and tables (+ 8 in appendix). Code and data available at: https://github.com/yanglanya980929/xPGTauLeap

papers.title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
papers.summary: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_θ(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_θ(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.
papers.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 20 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Code: https://daiyral.github.io/Empirical-Bayes-Flow-Matching-for-Continuous-Cryo-EM-Heterogeneity/

papers.title: Information content of the Gamow Teller Resonance: Bayesian inference with self-consistent Skyrme models
papers.summary: Many important charge-exchange weak processes, such as beta decays, double beta decays, and neutrino-nucleus and neutrino-nucleon reactions, are closely related to the spin- and isospin-dependent nuclear force, yet few of them can be precisely measured, or even observed, in terrestrial experiments. The Gamow-Teller resonance (GTR) in finite nuclei is one of the few experimental probes of this spin-isospin force. In a companion letter, we obtained the probability distribution of the Landau-Migdal parameter $G'_0$, which characterizes the main part of the spin-isospin force, from GTR measurements using Bayesian inference. In this follow-up work, we quantitatively study the correlations emerging from this Bayesian analysis. From the posterior, we identify two standard Skyrme parameterizations (nuSky*) that reproduce, in a unified manner, ground-state observables of finite nuclei, the salient features of the GTR, and the bulk properties of neutron-star matter. Since collective excitations in finite nuclei and in neutron-star matter are related, we use the Skyrme interactions sampled from the posterior to constrain the axial-current, charged-current neutrino-nucleon reaction rates in hot and dense compact-star matter, as the first astrophysical application of this study. The GTR-informed calculations substantially reduce the spread of the neutrino opacity; nevertheless, significant uncertainties remain due to the poorly constrained symmetry energy at sub-saturation densities. Constraining this quantity on top of a well-constrained spin-isospin interaction would pave the way towards a systematic determination of neutrino interactions in dense matter.
papers.comment: This paper has a joint article titled "Bayesian Inference of the Landau Parameter $G'_0$ from Joint Gamow-Teller Measurements"

papers.title: Ablating Design Choices for Protein Ensemble Generators Across Structural Regimes
papers.summary: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles inherit much of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins. Ordered and disordered proteins, however, occupy distinct structural regimes, and we investigate how design choices hold up across them. Using a minimal C$α$ flow-matching model, we ablate choices of architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training source, and evaluate each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data partitioned into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, a smaller protein language model performs worse on ordered proteins but not on disordered ones, and alignment in the loss degrades agreement with SAXS. Replacing coarse-grained simulations of disordered proteins with fragment-assembled ensembles improves agreement with chemical shifts at a cost to SAXS, while an equal mixture of the two keeps most of the gain at a smaller cost. This points to the training data, rather than the architecture, as the main constraint.

papers.title: Observation of Scaling of Higher-Order Flow in a Unitary Fermi Gas
papers.summary: Collective flow emerging from spatially anisotropic many-body systems is a fundamental manifestation of strongly interacting quantum matter, from ultracold quantum gases to the quark-gluon plasma created in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Yet how collective flow emerges across different spatial harmonics and how dissipation modifies its evolution remain largely unexplored. Here we investigate the nonequilibrium expansion of a unitary Fermi gas initially confined in nearly homogeneous potentials with engineered angular deformations. By suddenly releasing the confinement, we resolve anisotropic flow harmonics up to the seventh order. Remarkably, after normalization and rescaling by the characteristic expansion timescale, the different harmonics and system sizes exhibit a universal early-time evolution. At longer times, this universality breaks down and we observe an approximately quadratic dependence of the harmonic attenuation on harmonic order, consistent with viscous acoustic scaling. Furthermore, temperature-dependent measurements reveal the role of shear viscosity in the dissipative evolution of higher-order flow. Our results open a new route to exploring the interplay between universal hydrodynamic expansion and dissipative transport, connecting collective dynamics in ultracold quantum gases with anisotropic flow in strongly interacting nuclear matter.

papers.title: Pionization experiments in light nuclei
papers.summary: The zero-energy antiproton absorption in light nuclei is considered. The ratios $R_{n/p}$ of antiproton-neutron versus antiproton-proton capture rates in the lightest nuclei $^2$H, $^3$He and $^4$He are analyzed, both from the experimental results and from some selected theoretical models. These models are used as key input in determining the level shifts and widths of the lowest states. We establish the capture orbit in $^3$He to be states of angular momentum $L=2$. Several N-N optical potentials are used to compute the $R_{n/p}$ values for several heavy nuclei and the results are found to be consistent with the data. However, the old chamber experiments studying pionization in Helium, are not consistent with models. Only the Paris potential is likely to succeed provided baryonia states predicted by this model are better understood.
papers.comment: To appear in Phys Rev C

papers.title: Basic Reproductive Numbers in Host-Parasite Systems with Demographic Bistability
papers.summary: The basic reproductive number, $\mathcal{R}_0$, is widely used to determine whether an infectious disease can persist in a population. However, its interpretation may become unclear when the underlying disease-free demographic dynamics exhibit multiple types of stable attractors. In this study, we investigate how demographic bistability between fixed points and periodic cycles affects the calculation and interpretation of $\mathcal{R}_0$. We consider two discrete-time host-parasite models with infection: a tick-host model motivated by Borrelia burgdorferi transmission and a Nicholson-Bailey host-parasitoid model with intraspecific competition and infection. For each model, we calculate reproductive numbers associated with different disease-free attractors using the next-generation operator method and compare their invasion thresholds. In the tick-host model, the reproduction number calculated on the stable demographic cycle differs from that calculated at the positive coexistence fixed point, resulting in parameter regions where infection can invade at one demographic attractor but not the other. In contrast, in the host-parasitoid model, the host-driven invasion threshold is necessarily the same at the positive coexistence fixed point and on the host-only periodic cycles. These contrasting results demonstrate that demographic bistability alone does not necessarily produce attractor-dependent invasion thresholds. Rather, the effect of demographic dynamics on invasion depends on the structure of pathogen transmission. In particular, a complete host--vector--host transmission pathway can allow differences between demographic attractors to alter the invasion threshold. Our results emphasize the importance of considering both demographic dynamics and transmission structure when interpreting $\mathcal{R}_0$ in populations with multiple stable disease-free states.

papers.title: Deep Learning for Longitudinal Asymmetry in Heavy-Ion Collisions at RHIC Energies
papers.summary: We developed a deep neural network framework to predict the longitudinal asymmetry and the corresponding rapidity shift in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The model was trained using sufficiently large datasets for Au+Au and Cu+Cu collision systems at center-of-mass energies of 62.4 and 200 AGeV at RHIC. It successfully learns the underlying relationships between the input parameters and reconstructs the corresponding target quantities with good precision. Its predictions agree well with theoretical simulations across both trained and untrained centrality intervals. The influence of longitudinal asymmetry on final-state flow observables has also been studied, and the model results are in reasonable agreement with the simulation. A SHAP-based correlation analysis further supports the physical consistency of the learned feature dependencies and suggests that the observed correlations are not primarily driven by feature redundancy. The proposed framework provides a computationally efficient approach to estimating event-by-event results, potentially reducing the computational cost of large-scale theoretical model simulations. This work presents an initial study exploring the use of deep neural networks to investigate longitudinal asymmetry and rapidity shifts in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

papers.title: Cumulative protons and pions at the intermediate energies in the FRAGM experiment
papers.summary: One of the important research objectives of the FRAGM experiment operating at the TWAC heavy-ion accelerator-storage complex was the study of particle production in the cumulative region. Differential cross sections were measured for the production of pions - resulting from the fragmentation of carbon nuclei at an energy of 3.2 GeV/nucleon, as well as protons with energy range from 300 to 2000 MeV/nucleon at an angle of 3.5 degrees relative to the incident ion beam. The parameterization of cumulative effect used in experiments investigating nucleus-nucleus interactions is discussed. It is shown, that the energy dependencies of these parameters are analogous to those observed in nucleon-nucleus interactions and indicate the presence of nuclear scaling behavior.

papers.title: Investigating nucleon resonances in the $pp\to K^+K^+ΛΛ$ reaction
papers.summary: In this work, we investigate the \(pp \to K^+ K^+ ΛΛ\) reaction using an effective Lagrangian approach and the isobar model. The calculation includes the exchange of \(π\), \(η\), \(σ\), \(ρ\), \(ω\), and \(K\) mesons, as well as contributions from eight nucleon resonances: \(N(1535)\), \(N(1650)\), \(N(1710)\), \(N(1720)\), \(N(1895)\), \(N(1900)\), \(N(2060)\) and \(N(2120)\). The double-resonance excitation mechanism (\(NN \to N^* N^*\)) is found to dominate this reaction over the entire energy range considered. Among the exchanged mesons, the \(η\) exchange provides the largest contribution at lower energies, whereas the \(K\) exchange dominates at higher energies. Near the threshold, \(N(1535)\) and \(N(1650)\) play the most important roles, while at higher energies \(N(1710)\) and \(N(1720)\) become dominant. Due to isospin conservation, this reaction is predominantly coupled to nucleon resonances, providing a relatively clean channel for \(N^*\) spectroscopy. Our results indicate the unique potential of this reaction for studying nucleon resonances and provide a theoretical reference for future experimental studies at HIAF.

papers.title: Can multi-level Monte-Carlo address the sign problem in a finite-density Bose gas?
papers.summary: Numerical simulation of field theories with complex actions is frustrated by the sign problem, which causes an exponential growth in statistical sampling noise. A key example of such a theory is QCD at finite baryon chemical potential, which has important applications to the structure of atomic nuclei and neutron stars. Until now, the sign problem has precluded the possibility of first-principles numerical calculations that could provide key insight into these important physical systems. In this work, we propose an approach to avoiding this limitation by applying a reweighting procedure coupled with a multi-level Monte-Carlo sampling algorithm that offers an exponential enhancement of statistics to counteract the sign problem. We test the approach on a simpler model that displays the same sign problem at finite chemical potential. Our results demonstrate the promise of the proposed approach, significantly increasing the range over which precise calculations are possible, and providing improvements all the way up to the phase transition.

papers.title: Precise and accurate nuclear electric quadrupole moment of $^{223}$Ra from molecular spectroscopy
papers.summary: Nuclear electric quadrupole moments of unstable isotopes are commonly extracted from laser spectroscopy of the atomic hyperfine structure, where the accuracy is limited to the several-percent level by the available electric-field-gradient (EFG) calculations. In this study, we determine the spectroscopic quadrupole moment of $^{223}$Ra (half-life $t_{1/2} = 11.4$ d) from hyperfine-resolved collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy of the radioactive molecule $^{223}$Ra$^{19}$F. The $X\,^2Σ^+$ electronic ground state of RaF provides a large axial EFG at the radium nucleus that can be calculated with relativistic coupled-cluster theory to sub-percent accuracy. Together with a three-fold improvement in spectral resolution over previous fast-beam measurements of radioactive molecules, this yields $Q_s = +1.211(7)_\mathrm{stat}(2)_\mathrm{syst}(5)_\mathrm{theo}\,e\mathrm{b}$ for $^{223}$Ra with a total uncertainty of 0.73%, approximately three times better than atomic and ionic determinations. This result demonstrates that molecular spectroscopy can provide access to the electromagnetic structure of unstable nuclei with a precision competitive with, and in favorable cases better than, atomic spectroscopy, and may thus be envisioned for studies beyond the limitations of current radioactive-atom experiments.

papers.title: Curriculum unlearning in humans and neural networks
papers.summary: During learning, humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions. However, we lack a computational explanation for this phenomenon. Here, using a canonical behavioural task and modelling with neural networks, we develop and test a theory for why simple-to-complex curricula succeed. We show that during learning, both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, a tendency to learn simple rules that are underfit to the data. In neural networks this bias is accompanied by compression of neural representations. Simple-to-complex curricula help both types of learners overcome this compression, developing representations (and policy) with appropriate dimensionality for the task. We test and confirm a further prediction from this theory: learners that have been pre-exposed to simple tasks and with more compressed initial representations benefit more from curricula. These findings suggest that curricula help with ``unlearning'' of simple rules.

papers.title: Non-uniqueness of the amplitude reconstruction in the inverse scattering problem and a refinement of Hoehler's resonance clustering
papers.summary: Reaction-amplitude reconstruction in the inverse scattering problem is limited by the bilinear form of all reaction observables. At fixed kinematics, N complex amplitudes contain 2N real quantities, whereas complete measurements determine at most 2N-1 parameters. Uniqueness therefore depends on whether additional physical constraints, such as unitarity, supply the missing information. We examine the consequences for resonance identification, focusing on angular-momentum assignments. Building on published results showing how truncation redistributes pole-bearing contributions among effective partial waves, we examine exact and practical ambiguities associated with imposing coupled-channel unitarity. A 4 x 4 counterexample shows that different on-shell unitary amplitudes can produce identical measurable bilinears. Practical unitary descriptions can also yield different pole content while remaining compatible with experimental uncertainties. We update Hoehler's clustering using the thirteen four-star N* resonances in PDG 2026 and Bonn-Gatchina results published in 2025. Nearby poles with different partial-wave assignments occur both in the PDG compilation and within Bonn-Gatchina, so their proximity is not solely a consequence of PDG averaging. Some groupings persist, while others change appreciably. We discuss a conditional interpretation in which truncation redistributes a common pole-bearing contribution among effective partial waves, with additional reconstruction uncertainties potentially accounting for departures from coincident pole positions. These considerations allow, but do not establish, a common origin for cluster members. The necessity of separate states and the stability of their angular-momentum assignments remain questions for further investigation.

papers.title: Modeling fragmentation of $^{20}$Ne nuclei at the LHC
papers.summary: Fragmentation of relativistic neon nuclei was studied with the Abrasion-Ablation Monte Carlo for Colliders model (AAMCC-MST), which incorporates pre-equilibrium clustering of spectator matter via a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) algorithm, subsequent decays of the excited clusters, and Coulomb repulsion between final fragments. After validating the model against data on $^{20}$Ne and $^{22}$Ne fragmentation on various targets, the production of spectator nuclear fragments, neutrons, and protons in $^{20}$Ne-$^{20}$Ne collisions at the LHC was modeled at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.36$ TeV. The production cross sections, transverse and longitudinal momentum distributions for $^2$H, $^4$He, $^6$Li, $^{10}$B, $^{12}$C, $^{14}$N, and $^{16}$O fragments were calculated as these fragments may contaminate $^{20}$Ne beams circulating in the LHC. A simple parametrization describing relative width of the longitudinal momentum distributions calculated for these fragment species was constructed. To study the sensitivity of results to $α$-clustering and nuclear density distributions in neon nuclei, two density profiles for $^{20}$Ne and $^{22}$Ne were used: a deformed Woods-Saxon, and a five-$α$ bi-pyramidal configuration. In addition, a spherical profile was considered for $^{20}$Ne. Comparing results obtained with these profiles and with or without MST clustering shows that the calculated yields of spectator nucleons and fragments, their momentum distributions are sensitive to the details of nuclear structure of $^{20,22}$Ne and fragmentation modeling. The results provide the input for simulations of the transport of secondary forward nuclei in the LHC to estimate their interaction rates with circulating $^{20}$Ne beam nuclei, and also for calculations of responses of neutron and proton Zero Degree Calorimeters to $^{20}$Ne-$^{20}$Ne events.

papers.title: Trail systems self-organize through individual route optimization
papers.summary: As animals, including humans, walk, they compact the vegetation and ground beneath them, reducing the cost of movement for subsequent travelers. From this positive feedback emerge networks of trails which allow for efficient movement and store generational-scale information about the environment. Models simulating this process show how individuals following local cues produce trail systems with many of the features of real-world networks. However, little has been done to investigate walkers with more complete knowledge of their environment and the abilities to plan their behavior intelligently. Here we introduce a simple general model for trail formation, based on minimizing cost of movement by individuals. As in real environments, our simulations produce a striking variety of complex trail networks. We show that these trail systems optimally connect space according to the spatial needs of the walkers, that the geometry of those trail systems matches theoretical predictions and that the systems they generate may fall into multiple attracting states. As technological advances allow us to quantify trail systems across diverse habitats and species, our model provides a theoretical foundation for empirical research on animal trails and for understanding the emergence of human transportation networks, with implications for urban design.

papers.title: Predicting protein structures at any folding stage from sequence
papers.summary: Protein structure prediction has largely focused on native conformations, leaving the continuum of unfolded states, folding intermediates, and native structures difficult to access. We present FoldScape, a sequence-conditioned deep learning framework for generating protein conformational ensembles at specified folding fractions $Q$. Trained on approximately one million conformations from 10,000 protein sequences, FoldScape combines coarse-grained folding and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories. It reconstructs three-dimensional $C_α$ chains through hierarchical sliding-window regressions of inter-residue distances, chain-level assembly, and a rectified-flow decoder. By conditioning on folding progress, FoldScape generates conformations from unfolded states through intermediates to native-state structures without protein-specific molecular dynamics at inference. In matched-sample comparisons, FoldScape achieves median conformational-space coverage of 0.989, 0.722, and 0.877 along radius of gyration, fraction of native contacts $Q$, and secondary-structure fraction, respectively, versus 0.05, 0.05, and 0.10 for seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles. Coverage advantages are consistent across the evaluated proteins and robust to binning choices. Reconstruction accuracy remains approximately stable across the evaluated stages of a folding trajectory, and stride-one crop-and-superpose inference extends predictions to chains several times longer than the single-pass limit. Analyses of mechanical-unfolding trajectories show residue-resolved pathways, reproducible extension-conditioned observables across pulling velocities, and geometrically coherent segments in partially unfolded chains. FoldScape extends sequence-based structure prediction beyond a single folded endpoint to controllable conformational-ensemble generation across protein folding.

papers.title: Carbon-Reaction Constraints on Stellar Evolution: White-Dwarf Heating, Carbon-Burning Products, and Black-Hole Masses
papers.summary: The effects of ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}+{}^{12}\mathrm{C}$ fusion and ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}(α,γ){}^{16}\mathrm{O}$ capture on stellar heating, composition, and black-hole masses are examined. Rates from a published Bayesian analysis of carbon fusion are used in calculations with MESA. In an accreting carbon--oxygen white dwarf, the Bayesian rates move the point at which nuclear heating equals combined neutrino and surface photon losses to slightly larger stellar masses and higher central temperatures and densities. At an accretion rate of $10^{-7}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, the Bayesian median gives a central temperature approximately $2.57\%$ higher and a central density $18.9\%$ higher than the calculation using the standard CF88 rate. A separate calculation follows carbon burning in an initially $20\,M_\odot$, $Z=0.0142$ star. Relative to the CF88 rate with MESA's standard division between proton and alpha channels, the Bayesian-median rate with the proton-to-alpha ratio of Yang et al. increases the neon-20 mass remaining at central carbon depletion by $10.8\%$ and decreases the sodium-23 mass by $28.7\%$. For helium capture on carbon, the nuclear constraint $S_{\rm tot}(300\,\mathrm{keV})=118\pm17\,\mathrm{keV\,b}$ is applied to the published $Z=10^{-5}$ stellar models of Farag et al. Linear interpolation gives a maximum black-hole mass below the pair-instability gap of approximately $61.5$--$77.4\,M_\odot$ within the assumptions of those models. New MESA calculations at $Z=0.00142$ give smaller bound masses before collapse. Differences in the stellar assumptions prevent attributing the difference between the two curves to metallicity alone.

papers.title: Evolving view on phylogenetic networks
papers.summary: Reticulate processes such as hybridization, introgression, and horizontal gene transfer cannot be fully represented by a bifurcating tree. Enter phylogenetic networks: first as split graphs to visualize tree discordance, then as explicit probabilistic models that capture biological phenomena. Here, we describe the broad taxonomy of network representations, distinguishing the principal classes of explicit networks, their biological interpretability and our ability to accurately estimate them from empirical data. We also trace the evolution of the main network inferential methods from hybrid detection tests, distance- and subgraph-based amalgamation methods, probabilistic approaches under the multispecies network coalescent, composite-likelihood and divide-and-conquer frameworks, while highlighting the selective pressures of statistical identifiability and computational scalability that have shaped this evolution. As we move towards a network thinking paradigm, previously isolated methodological lineages from population genetics, phylogenomics, and mathematical network theory are now introgressing, uniting diverse network models into a shared framework that can integrate sequence- and species-level reticulate processes, increase robustness to systematic errors, and refine algorithms for genome-scale data, expanding the tree of life into a richer, more entangled yet clearer picture of evolution.

papers.title: GINsim 3.1: Qualitative modelling and dynamical analysis of logical regulatory networks
papers.summary: GINsim is a software for the definition and dynamical analysis of qualitative (Boolean and multi-valued) models of biological regulatory networks. Building on its modular architecture, based on the MDDlib decision-diagram and bioLQM model-manipulation libraries, GINsim version 3.1 introduces new functionalities aimed at the analysis of large logical models: the symbolic computation of trap-spaces, the Booleanisation of multilevel models and the reversal of model dynamics. GINsim 3.1 also extends the estimation of attractor reachability (Monte Carlo and Avatar algorithms), the computation of stable states, as well as model reduction functionalities. Analyses can be applied to perturbed models, and scripted, in particular from the CoLoMoTo interactive notebook. We illustrate the main functionalities of GINsim on a reference multilevel model of regulatory network that control the mammalian cell cycle, including the computation of its stable states and cyclic attractor, the assessment of their reachability, and the identification of the regulatory circuits driving multistability and oscillations. GINsim is freely available under GPL-3.0 at https://ginsim.github.io/, runs on any platform supporting Java, and is interoperable with the other tools of the CoLoMoTo community. Its website provides installation instructions and reference documentation, as well as a repository of Boolean and multilevel logical models.
papers.comment: 22 pages, 3 tables, 5 figures. Submitted to npj systems biology

papers.title: When Model Complexity Matters in Cross-Subject Naturalistic fMRI Prediction
papers.summary: Increasingly complex neural models predict blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses to naturalistic stimuli, but the predictive value of this added complexity remains unclear. We ask when pretrained stimulus representations help and how much downstream complexity is needed, with and without recent measured BOLD history. We compare linear diagnostic references and nonlinear predictors across HCP movie fMRI (154 subjects), BOLD Moments (10 subjects), and Algonauts 2025 (4 subjects). Under a shared offline protocol, models are fitted on training subjects and evaluated on held-out subjects viewing largely familiar stimuli, without refitting. Pretrained visual features generally improve prediction over raw pixels; for linear autoregression, this advantage becomes more pronounced over longer rollouts (recursive predictions without additional measured BOLD). Measured BOLD history provides substantial gains that generally diminish {as rollouts lengthen}. Nonlinear stimulus-only predictors can improve on linear readouts, whereas linear autoregression provides a strong history-conditioned baseline. Controls examine context length, regularization, fitting procedures, and model capacity. Regional response consistency across subjects is associated with held-out prediction accuracy, while less consistent regions tend to gain more from measured history. In paired simulations with fixed linear neural dynamics, slower hemodynamic responses generally sustain high temporal prediction correlations over longer rollouts, illustrating how the observation process can contribute to predictive persistence. Together, these findings support evaluating stimulus representations and downstream complexity separately, using history-conditioned linear prediction as a diagnostic reference under matched inputs and measurement availability.

papers.title: Visualization and Characterization of Gene Group Distribution Patterns Across Genomes
papers.summary: Genes of the same family often lie close together on a chromosome, yet how far apart family members sit, and whether their spacing follows any pattern, has rarely been measured consistently across genomes. We built an interactive web application that places the members of any of the 1,396 FlyBase gene groups on the banded ideogram of the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) and lists each member's neighbours. While browsing it, we found strikingly symmetric gene sets in which consecutive members are almost evenly spaced. In the RAB GTPases, two 5.08 Mb spacings differ by only 634 bp. We also found that distances between neighbouring members fall into two populations: short-range (median 1.8 kb) and long-range (median 2.4 Mb). Although an arm-matched random control suggests that the even spacing (without a minimum-distance filter) as well as the long-range population arise largely by chance, the short-range population turns out to be a genuine clustering signal. We then extended the analysis to human and six other model organisms (mouse, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis thaliana and maize), and every genome showed the same two populations. The mixture curve of the two is nearly constant across chromosomes in some genomes (Type I: fly, maize, Arabidopsis, C. elegans) but varies across chromosomes in others (Type II: human, mouse, zebrafish, yeast). Thus, across eight eukaryotes, family members lie in two distance populations. The scale of the short-range population follows the spacing of genes in each genome, and the long-range population matches random placement in fly and is consistent with it in the other genomes. Our results also show that visual patterns such as even spacing must be tested against chance before they are interpreted. Our tool and approach give a simple way to explore and compare gene clustering across species.

papers.title: Quasi-normal Modes and Instabilities of Rotating Relativistic Stars
papers.summary: We derive the basic equations suitable for the coupled fluid--spacetime eigenvalue problem from the second-order action in full general relativity and accurately determine quasi-normal modes of a variety of rapidly rotating stars with outgoing-wave boundary conditions. For MIT-bag strange stars, the spectrum realizes Chandrasekhar's instability picture, with distinct Chandrasekhar--Friedman--Schutz and Jacobi-like neutral conditions and the transition to dynamical bar-mode growth. For neutron stars, we determine the $f$-, $r$-, and other inertial-mode spectra and their radiative damping or growth times. Interactions between $f$- and inertial modes reveal avoided crossings and exchanges for radiative damping or growth rates. We locate quasiradial collapse thresholds through a static stability analysis and independently verify them by tracking the fundamental $F$-mode frequency to zero, clarifying that the central density at the onset of the dynamical instability is always larger than that of the secular instability for uniform rotation. Our formalism and numerical implementation can also resolve highly damped $w$-modes.

papers.title: Hydrogen Electron Cyclotron Resonance Dissociator Demonstrator for the Project 8 Experiment
papers.summary: Project 8, a neutrino mass experiment, employs the novel frequency technique of cyclotron radiation emission spectroscopy (CRES) to perform a model independent measurement of neutrino mass via tritium beta decay. Our pioneering experiment will consist of a beamline that dissociates molecular tritium, surface cools atoms through accommodation, evaporatively cools and slows atoms, and traps them in a CRES resonant cavity to advance towards our sensitivity goal of 40 meV/c^2 for our final electron-weighted neutrino mass measurement. We are prototyping an electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) dissociator that uses a tunable 1 kW 2.45 GHz RF generator and electromagnets to ignite a hydrogen plasma in an aluminum resonant cavity. Our ECR source is designed to produce a high atom flux (~10^19 atoms/second) near room temperature. We present the engineering development, gas diagnostics, and spectroscopy data from our hydrogen plasma.

papers.title: Parametrization of unitary matrices, parametrizing the symmetric $S$ matrix and the $NN$ $S$ matrix above the inelastic threshold
papers.summary: None of the $S$-matrix representations used in analyses of nucleon-nucleon ($NN$) scattering above the inelastic threshold is implicitly unitary, general, and connected to low-energy (Stapp) parameters, and hence correspondingly related to the physical properties of the scattering. Such a representation is also needed to solve the corresponding inverse scattering problem. I present an $S$-matrix representation which satisfies these requirements. As a by-product, I derive a parametrization of an $n$-dimensional unitary matrix.

papers.title: One Mistake, Three Layers: Persistence Rules Under Depth Correlation
papers.summary: Probing frozen representations layer by layer is now standard practice, but reporting when a signal first becomes decodable requires a rule for reading a depth curve, and the obvious rule is wrong. On synthetic curves with known ground truth, requiring a probe score to exceed a null-calibrated threshold for three consecutive stages reports an onset nineteen stages early under transformer-like depth correlation, with every resample returning an onset. The failure follows from correlation between neighboring layers, a hazard known in neuroimaging but not, to our knowledge, checked for depth curves. We give an estimator whose error rate is calibrated rather than assumed. Null trajectories are built by permuting labels within each evaluation unit and holding each permutation fixed across depth, preserving the correlation structure the rule must survive; thresholds are per-layer order statistics; and the persistence requirement is calibrated rather than chosen. Applied to pocket information in a frozen co-folding trunk, stratifying 1,820 post-cutoff targets by protein-family and pocket familiarity, the five-stage rule fires on 4 to 7 per cent of null trajectories against a nominal 5 per cent and the three-stage rule on 12 to 17: the synthetic failure reproduces on real data. Pocket membership is decodable above threshold at all 48 blocks in all four regimes, so the onset cannot discriminate them; the pre-declared accumulation depth does, and is latest for familiar families with structurally novel pockets in every feature set. That regime is also the weakest, by a margin surviving controls for length, pocket measure and alignment depth. Separately, a widely used public co-folding checkpoint loads against its own code with 128 trunk parameters missing; those would be randomly initialized, and every representation extracted would be partly noise while appearing normal.

papers.title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
papers.summary: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.

papers.title: Fly Whiskers Meet LiDAR: Robust Navigation under Sensor Failure
papers.summary: We extend FLYNN, a leaky integrator recurrent network wired on the Drosophila melanogaster connectome, with a 32-ray 2D LiDAR interface that requires no learned fusion layer beyond a scalar input gain. A 270 degree frontal scan at 8 m range is injected as inverted proximity into the 37 BM Vib head-bristle neurons. Across 24 paired comparisons in a four- state vision matrix with LiDAR on or off, FLYNN-LiDAR has 17 significant wins, 5 nonsignificant comparisons, and 2 significant losses against three LiDAR-capable baselines. Both losses are to MobileNet with the left eye off. With full vision, FLYNN- LiDAR reaches 96.6% success. Under total vision loss, the scan raises success from 45.2% to 64.6%; the baselines reach 44.6% to 56.6% with the scan on. Under out of distribution textures, it is the only LiDAR-capable model whose success improves with the scan (44.2% to 58.4%); both CNNs score 0%, and SmallWorld declines from 26.8% to 7.4%. Under periodic vision dropout, FLYNN-LiDAR achieves 93.6% and 89.6% success at 25% and 50% duty with fewer collisions. Profiling the evaluated forward paths gives 3.93M multiply accumulate operations per step; EfficientNet and MobileNet require 4.60x and 2.94x as many. Final- state analysis shows near-linear sensory superposition (cosine 0.9955).

papers.title: Active-subspace learning reveals dominant parameter directions in nuclear observables
papers.summary: Nuclear observables computed using ab initio methods can depend on many low-energy constants (LECs) of the underlying chiral effective field theory interactions, while being sensitive to only a few LEC combinations. We use active-subspace learning to identify these dominant parameter directions directly from many-body calculations. For ground-state energies and charge radii of oxygen isotopes, we find that more than 99% of the gradient-based variation is concentrated along a single direction for each observable in the 17-dimensional LEC space. Comparing these directions across nuclei and observables quantifies similarities in their LEC dependence. The same analysis yields derivative-based global sensitivities without requiring a global emulator. Active-subspace directions can also serve as an efficient representation for emulation, greatly improving Gaussian-process emulators especially for broad LEC variations. We demonstrate this for Hartree-Fock calculations of $^{48}\mathrm{Ca}$, where the emulator error is improved with active-subspace learning by more than two orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Differential measurement of global polarization of $Λ$, $Ξ$, and $Ω$ hyperons in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=7.7$--$27~\mathrm{GeV}$ from the RHIC Beam Energy Scan-II
papers.summary: We present high-precision differential measurements of the global polarization of $Λ$, $Ξ$, and $Ω$ hyperons in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=7.7$, $9.2$, $11.5$, $14.6$, $17.3$, $19.6$, and $27~\mathrm{GeV}$ from the RHIC Beam Energy Scan Phase II (BES-II) using the STAR detector. The results show a clear centrality dependence, with polarization increasing toward more peripheral collisions. Within the present experimental precision, no significant dependence on transverse momentum is observed for $Λ$ and $Ξ$, and no significant rapidity dependence is observed for the $Ξ$. The polarization of $Ξ$ hyperons is comparable at the current precision to that of $Λ$ hyperons, consistent with a picture in which all hyperons acquire polarization from the same global angular momentum source, with differences arising from quark content and hadronization dynamics. These high-precision, differential measurements across centrality and $p_T$ over the measured energy ranges provide a unique test of spin--vorticity coupling and sensitivity to spin--spin correlations among hyperons with different quark content (uds, dss, and sss). The results are consistent, within current precision and under the stated spin-transfer assumptions, with a common vorticity-driven polarization mechanism across strange and multistrange hyperons. Consequently, they constrain the interplay of vorticity, magnetic fields, and quark-flavor dynamics in the produced medium.
